Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 7, verse 65–72:

And to ʿAd [We sent] their brother Hud. Meaning: We sent to ʿAd, hence the accusative in "akhahum" (their brother). He was ʿAlaʾ ibn ʿAwṣ ibn Adam ibn Sam ibn Nuh, and he is the first ʿAd. [He was] their brother by lineage, not in religion: Hud, who was Hud ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Riyah ibn al-Khulud ibn ʿAd ibn ʿAwṣ ibn Adam ibn Sam ibn Nuh. Ibn Ishaq said: Hud ibn [Shalikh] ibn Arfakhshad ibn Sam ibn Nuh. He said to them: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. Will you not fear Allah?" meaning, that you single Him out and worship Him. The chiefs of those of his people who disbelieved said: "Indeed we see you in folly," meaning ignorance and misguidance [by your abandoning our religion], "and indeed we think you are among the liars," [that] you are the messenger of Allah to us, and that the punishment is descending upon us. He said: "O my people, there is no folly in me, but I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds. I convey to you the messages of my Lord, and I am a sincere adviser to you," calling you to repentance, "trustworthy." Al-Dahhak said: trustworthy regarding the message. Al-Kalbi said: I was among you before this [day], trustworthy. "Are you amazed that a reminder from your Lord has come to you through a man from among you," meaning himself, "to warn you? And remember when He made you successors after the people of Nuh," meaning: after He destroyed them [for their associating partners with Him], "and increased you in stature and build," that is, in height, strength and might.

Muqatil said: the height of each man was twelve cubits. Ibn ʿAbbas: [it was] the size of one cubit. Al-Kalbi said: the tallest of them was a hundred cubits and the shortest sixty cubits. Abu Hamza al-Thumali: seventy cubits. Ibn ʿAbbas: eighty. Wahb: the head of one of them was like a great dome, and a man's eye would be a nest in which beasts bred, and likewise their nostrils. "So remember the bounties of Allah," the blessings of Allah. Its singular is [il, ili, ilu, ila, like al-ana; its singular is inn, inni, innu, anni] [[Addition from the tafsir of al-Qurtubi: 7/237.]] "that you may prosper." They said: "Have you come to us that we should worship Allah alone and leave what our fathers used to worship," and abandon what our fathers used to worship of idols, "so bring us what you threaten us with," meaning the punishment, "if you are of the truthful." He said: "Punishment has already come upon you from your Lord, [a rijs]," that is, punishment, "and wrath." [The sin is the origin of the zay] [[As in the manuscript; the meaning is that rijz with zay and rijs with sin have the same meaning, the sin being changed to zay; this is the view of Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla. See Zad al-Masir: 3/151.]] "Do you dispute with me concerning names you have named, which you have set upon idols [ ... ] [[Illegible word.]] worshipping fire, you and your fathers before you? Allah has sent down no authority for them," no proof, clarification or evidence. "So wait; I am with you among those who wait." Then We saved him, meaning Hud, at the descent of the punishment.

"And those with him by a mercy from Us, and We cut off the root of those who denied Our signs," that is, We uprooted them and destroyed them entirely, "and they were not believers."

The account of ʿAd and their destruction, as related by Muhammad ibn Ishaq, al-Suddi and others of the narrators and exegetes, is that ʿAd dwelt in Yemen, and their dwellings were there at al-Shajara and al-Ahqaf, which are sands called the sands of ʿAlij, and Dumma and Birin [[Birin: a village of Homs; Dumma: a village below al-Anbar on the Euphrates.]], between ʿUman and Hadramawt. Along with that they had spread throughout the land, subdued it and oppressed its people by virtue of the strength that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, had given them. They were worshippers of idols besides Allah: an idol called Sana, an idol called Samud, and an idol called al-Hubar.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent to them Hud as a prophet. He was of the most noble of them in lineage and the most excellent of them in descent. He commanded them to single out Allah and not to associate with Him any other god, and to refrain from wronging people, [and he did not] command them, as is related, to anything other than that.

But they refused him and denied him, and they said: "Who is mightier than us in strength?" They built monuments and seized by force like tyrants, as Allah the Exalted mentioned. When they did that, Allah withheld the rain from them for three years, until it afflicted them severely.

In that era, when calamity or war befell people, they would call upon Allah for relief and seek Allah's help at the Sacred House in Mecca, Muslim and polytheist alike. Many diverse peoples of differing religions would gather in Mecca, and all of them held Mecca in reverence, knowing its sanctity and its standing with Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The people of Mecca at that time were the Amaliq; they were called Amaliq because their father was ʿAmliq ibn Lawdh ibn Sam ibn Nuh. The chief of the Amaliq in Mecca at that time was a man called Muʿawiya ibn Bakr, and the mother of Muʿawiya was Kalhada, daughter of [al-Khaybari], a man from the Greater ʿAd. When the rain was withheld from ʿAd and they were stricken, he said: "Prepare a delegation to [seek rain] for you." They sent Qayl ibn ʿUnuz, Laqim ibn Hazal, ʿUtayl ibn Dadd ibn ʿAd the Greater, and Marthad ibn Saʿd ibn ʿUqayr.

Marthad was a Muslim who concealed his Islam, and Jalhama ibn al-Khaybari [was also there]. Muʿawiya ibn Bakra said: Then they sent Luqman ibn ʿAd ibn Sad ibn ʿAd the Greater. Each man of these people set out with a group from his people, until they reached a number [and he counted them] of seventy men. When they came to Mecca, they stayed with Muʿawiya ibn Bakr, who was outside Mecca, outside the sacred precinct. He lodged them and honored them, for they were his brothers and in-laws. They stayed with him a month drinking wine, while two singing girls belonging to Muʿawiya ibn Bakr, called al-Jaradatan, sang to them. Their journey had been a month and their stay a month. When Muʿawiya ibn Bakr saw how long they stayed, though their people had sent them seeking relief from the calamity that had befallen them, he pitied them for it and said: "My brothers and in-laws have perished, and these stay with me as my guests. By Allah, I do not know how to deal with them. I am ashamed to order them to leave for what they were sent for, lest they think I am weary of their staying with me. And those behind them among their people have perished from drought and thirst." He complained of their situation to his two singing girls, the Jaradatan, and they said: "Compose a poem that we may sing, which they will not know who said it; perhaps that will stir them."

Muʿawiya ibn Bakr said:

Perhaps Allah will give us rain as clouds... Oh Qayl, woe to you, rise and make supplication.

They have become unable to speak... so let Him water the land of ʿAd, for ʿAd...

From the fierce thirst; there is no hope for us... neither the aged shaykh nor the youth.

Their women have become sick... and their women were in good state.

The wild beasts come to them openly... and no shafts fear for ʿAd.

You are here, in what you desire... your day and your night are complete.

Wretched is your delegation from a people... they neither greet nor give salutation.

When he had recited the poem, the two singing girls sang it to them. When the people heard it, some said to others: "Your people sent you only seeking relief from you from this calamity that has descended upon them, and you have delayed too long. Enter this sanctuary and ask for water for your people." Marthad ibn Saʿd ibn ʿUqayr said: "By Allah, you will not be watered by your supplications, but if you obey your prophet and turn in repentance to Him, you will be watered." He then openly declared his Islam. Jalhama ibn [al-Khaybari], the maternal uncle of Muʿawiya, when he heard his words and knew that he had followed the religion of Hud (peace be upon him), said:

Men of nobility, and your mother is from Thamud... O Abu Saʿd, you are from a tribe...

We will not obey you as long as we live... nor will we do what you wish.

Do you order us to abandon the religion of Rifd... and the sands of al-Sada with the Samud?

Men of opinion, and we follow the religion of Hud... and abandon the religion of noble fathers.

Then he said to Muʿawiya ibn Bakr and his father Bakr, who was an old shaykh: "Detain Marthad ibn Saʿd from us, so that he does not enter Mecca with us, for he has followed the religion of Hud and abandoned our religion."

Then they set out to Mecca to seek rain for ʿAd. When they turned toward Mecca, Marthad ibn Saʿd went out from the dwelling of Muʿawiya and caught up with them there, saying: "I will not supplicate Allah, Mighty and Majestic, for anything they set out for." When he reached them, he stood to supplicate Allah while they had gathered to call upon Allah, and he said: "O Allah, grant me my request alone, and do not include me in anything they ask of You." Qayl ibn ʿUnuz was at the head of the delegation of ʿAd, and the delegation of ʿAd said: "O Allah, grant him what he asks of You and make our request together with his request." He had [stayed behind] from the delegation of ʿAd when Luqman ibn ʿAd prayed, and he was the chief of ʿAd. When they had finished their supplication, he stood and said: "O Allah, I have come to You alone in my need, so grant me my request," and he asked Allah, Mighty and Majestic, for long life. He was granted the lifespan of seven vultures. Qayl ibn ʿUnuz said: "[O our God], if Hud is truthful, give us rain, for we are destroyed."

He said: "O Allah, I did not come for a sick man that I might treat him, nor for a captive that I might call to him. O Allah, water ʿAd with what You used to water them." Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, produced for him [clouds] of three kinds: white, red and black. Then a caller called from heaven: "O Qayl, choose for yourself and your people from this cloud whatever you wish." Qayl said: "I have chosen the black cloud, for it is the largest of clouds." The caller called to him: "You have chosen a whirlwind of ashes, dust upon dust, that will leave none of ʿAd, neither parent nor child, but will make them all ruins, except the sons of al-Luwdhiyya al-Muhdha."

The sons of al-Luwdhiyya are the sons of Luqaym ibn Hazal ibn Hazayla ibn Bakr. They were residents of Mecca with their maternal uncles, and they were not with ʿAd in their land. The other ʿAd were from the offspring of those of ʿAd who survived.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent forth the black cloud that Qayl had chosen, [containing vengeance] upon ʿAd, until it came out upon them from a valley of theirs called al-Mughith. When they saw it they rejoiced, and said: "This is a cloud bringing us rain." Allah the Exalted says: "Rather, it is that which you sought to hasten: a wind wherein is a painful punishment, destroying everything by the command of its Lord." [[Surat al-Ahqaf: 24–25.]]

The first to perceive what was in it and to recognise that it was a wind was a woman of ʿAd called Mahdar. When it came upon them, she cried out and fell unconscious. When she recovered, they said: "What did you see?" She said: "I saw its wind, and in it were sparks like fire, and before it were men leading it." "He subjected it against them for seven nights and eight days, in succession," [[Surat al-Haqqa: 7.]] that is, continuously. It left none of ʿAd alive except that they perished.

Hud (peace be upon him) and the believers with him withdrew into an enclosure where nothing afflicted them of that wind except what soothed the skins and delighted the souls. Indeed, it lifted up ʿAd and their households between heaven and earth and dashed them down with stones.

The delegation of ʿAd went out from Mecca until they passed by Muʿawiya ibn Bakr and stayed with him. While they were with him, a man came riding his camel on a moonlit night on the third evening after the calamity of ʿAd, and informed them of the news. They said to him: "Where did you leave Hud and his companions?" He said: "I left them at the shore of the sea," and it seems they doubted what he had told them. Hudhayla bint Bakr said:

"He has spoken truly, by the Lord of Mecca."

It is related that Marthad ibn Saʿd and Luqman ibn ʿAd, and it is said Qayl ibn ʿUnuz, when they supplicated in Mecca, were told: "You have been given your wishes; choose for yourselves, except that there is no way to immortality and death is inevitable." Mahd said: "O Allah, grant me righteousness and truthfulness," and it was granted. Luqman said: "Give me, O Lord, a lifespan," and it was said to him: "Choose for yourself the survival of seven she-goats, dark-coated, stubborn, in a rugged mountain that the rain does not touch, or the survival of seven vultures, when one vulture dies another comes after it." He chose seven vultures, and Luqman lived the lifespan of seven vultures: he would take the chick as soon as it hatched from its egg, and take the male of it for its sustenance, until it died, and then he would take another. He continued doing this until the seventh, and each vulture lived two hundred years, and the last of them was Labad. When Labad died, Luqman died with him.

As for Qayl, he chose that what had befallen his people should befall him too. It was said to him: "It is destruction," and he said: "I do not mind; I have no need of life after them," and what had befallen ʿAd of punishment befell him, and he perished. [[In full in the tafsir of al-Tabari: 8/282, no. 11493.]]

It is related from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: Allah revealed to the barren wind that it should go out against the people of ʿAd and take vengeance for Him upon them. It went out without measure, in the size of an ox's nostril, until the earth quaked from east to west. The treasurers said: "O Lord, we cannot withstand it; if it went out in its own state, it would destroy everything between the eastern and western ends of the earth." Allah revealed to it: "Return, and go out in the size of a ring's hole." So it returned and went out in the size of a ring's hole, and that is its creation. [[al-Durr al-Manthur: 3/96.]]

It is related from ʿAsim ibn ʿAmr and al-Bajali, from Abu Umama al-Bahili, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "A people of this community will spend the night over food, drink and frivolity, and in the morning they will be apes and swine, and a sinking and a stoning will befall them, and they will say: 'Last night so-and-so's house sank, and last night the house of so-and-so sank.' And the barren wind that destroyed ʿAd will surely be sent upon them, because of their drinking of wine, their consuming of usury, their taking of singing girls, their wearing of silk and their severing of the ties of kinship." [188] [[Tarikh Dimashq: 25/284.]]

And in a report: Of the wind there was sent upon them only the amount that flows through a ring. Al-Suddi said: Allah sent to ʿAd the barren wind. When it drew near them, they saw camels and men being carried through the air by the wind between heaven and earth. When they saw it, they hastened into their houses. When they entered the houses, it entered upon them and destroyed them within, then brought them out from the houses. When Allah had destroyed them, He sent upon them black birds which picked them up and cast them into the sea. No wind ever went out except by measure, except on that day; it rebelled against the treasurers and overturned them, so they did not know how much its measure was.

Abu al-Tufayl ʿAmir ibn Wathila said: I heard ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah honour his face, say to a man from Hadramawt: "Did you see a red sandhill mixed with red clay and abundant lote trees in such-and-such a region of Hadramawt?" He said: "Yes, O Commander of the Faithful. By Allah, you describe it as one who has seen it." He said: "But I have only heard of it." The Hadrami said: "What is its matter, O Commander of the Faithful?" He said: "In it is the grave of Hud, peace be upon him." [[al-Mustadrak: 2/564.]]

ʿAta ibn al-Sa'ib, from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, said: Between the Corner and the Station and Zamzam is the grave of ninety-nine prophets, and the graves of Hud, Shu'ayb, Salih and Isma'il are in that place.

In another narration: Whenever a prophet's people perished and he and the righteous with him were saved, he would go with those who were with him to Mecca, and they would worship Allah there until they died.

The account of ʿAd and their destruction, as related by Muhammad ibn Ishaq, al-Suddi and others of the narrators and exegetes, is that ʿAd dwelt in Yemen, and their dwellings were there at al-Shajara and al-Ahqaf, which are sands called the sands of ʿAlij, and Dumma and Birin [[Birin: a village of Homs; Dumma: a village below al-Anbar on the Euphrates.]], between ʿUman and Hadramawt. He commanded them to single out Allah and not to associate with Him any other god, and to refrain from wronging people, [and he did not] command them, as is related, to anything other than that.

But they refused him and denied him, and they said: "Who is mightier than us in strength?" They built monuments and seized by force like tyrants, as Allah the Exalted mentioned. When they did that, Allah withheld the rain from them for three years, until it afflicted them severely.

When they came to Mecca, they stayed with Muʿawiya ibn Bakr, who was outside Mecca, outside the sacred precinct. He lodged them and honored them, for they were his brothers and in-laws. They stayed with him a month drinking wine, while two singing girls belonging to Muʿawiya ibn Bakr, called al-Jaradatan, sang to them. Their journey had been a month and their stay a month. When Muʿawiya ibn Bakr saw how long they stayed, though their people had sent them seeking relief from the calamity that had befallen them, he pitied them for it and said: "My brothers and in-laws have perished, and these stay with me as my guests. By Allah, I do not know how to deal with them. I am ashamed to order them to leave for what they were sent for, lest they think I am weary of their staying with me. And those behind them among their people have perished from drought and thirst." He complained of their situation to his two singing girls, the Jaradatan, and they said: "Compose a poem that we may sing, which they will not know who said it; perhaps that will stir them."

Muʿawiya ibn Bakr said:

Perhaps Allah will give us rain as clouds... Oh Qayl, woe to you, rise and make supplication.

They have become unable to speak... so let Him water the land of ʿAd, for ʿAd...

From the fierce thirst; there is no hope for us... neither the aged shaykh nor the youth.

Their women have become sick... and their women were in good state.

The wild beasts come to them openly... and no shafts fear for ʿAd.

You are here, in what you desire... your day and your night are complete.

Wretched is your delegation from a people... they neither greet nor give salutation.

When he had recited the poem, the two singing girls sang it to them. When the people heard it, some said to others: "Your people sent you only seeking relief from you from this calamity that has descended upon them, and you have delayed too long. Enter this sanctuary and ask for water for your people." Marthad ibn Saʿd ibn ʿUqayr said: "By Allah, you will not be watered by your supplications, but if you obey your prophet and turn in repentance to Him, you will be watered." He then openly declared his Islam. Jalhama ibn [al-Khaybari], the maternal uncle of Muʿawiya, when he heard his words and knew that he had followed the religion of Hud (peace be upon him), said:

Men of nobility, and your mother is from Thamud... O Abu Saʿd, you are from a tribe...

We will not obey you as long as we live... nor will we do what you wish.

Do you order us to abandon the religion of Rifd... and the sands of al-Sada with the Samud?

Men of opinion, and we follow the religion of Hud... and abandon the religion of noble fathers.

Then he said to Muʿawiya ibn Bakr and his father Bakr, who was an old shaykh: "Detain Marthad ibn Saʿd from us, so that he does not enter Mecca with us, for he has followed the religion of Hud and abandoned our religion."

Then they set out to Mecca to seek rain for ʿAd. When they turned toward Mecca, Marthad ibn Saʿd went out from the dwelling of Muʿawiya and caught up with them there, saying: "I will not supplicate Allah, Mighty and Majestic, for anything they set out for." When he reached them, he stood to supplicate Allah while they had gathered to call upon Allah, and he said: "O Allah, grant me my request alone, and do not include me in anything they ask of You." Qayl ibn ʿUnuz was at the head of the delegation of ʿAd, and the delegation of ʿAd said: "O Allah, grant him what he asks of You and make our request together with his request." He had [stayed behind] from the delegation of ʿAd when Luqman ibn ʿAd prayed, and he was the chief of ʿAd. When they had finished their supplication, he stood and said: "O Allah, I have come to You alone in my need, so grant me my request," and he asked Allah, Mighty and Majestic, for long life. He was granted the lifespan of seven vultures. Qayl ibn ʿUnuz said: "[O our God], if Hud is truthful, give us rain, for we are destroyed."

He said: "O Allah, I did not come for a sick man that I might treat him, nor for a captive that I might call to him. O Allah, water ʿAd with what You used to water them." Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, produced for him [clouds] of three kinds: white, red and black. Then a caller called from heaven: "O Qayl, choose for yourself and your people from this cloud whatever you wish." Qayl said: "I have chosen the black cloud, for it is the largest of clouds." The caller called to him: "You have chosen a whirlwind of ashes, dust upon dust, that will leave none of ʿAd, neither parent nor child, but will make them all ruins, except the sons of al-Luwdhiyya al-Muhdha."

The sons of al-Luwdhiyya are the sons of Luqaym ibn Hazal ibn Hazayla ibn Bakr. They were residents of Mecca with their maternal uncles, and they were not with ʿAd in their land. The other ʿAd were from the offspring of those of ʿAd who survived.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent forth the black cloud that Qayl had chosen, [containing vengeance] upon ʿAd, until it came out upon them from a valley of theirs called al-Mughith. When they saw it they rejoiced, and said: "This is a cloud bringing us rain." Allah the Exalted says: "Rather, it is that which you sought to hasten: a wind wherein is a painful punishment, destroying everything by the command of its Lord." [[Surat al-Ahqaf: 24–25.]]

The first to perceive what was in it and to recognise that it was a wind was a woman of ʿAd called Mahdar. When it came upon them, she cried out and fell unconscious. When she recovered, they said: "What did you see?" She said: "I saw its wind, and in it were sparks like fire, and before it were men leading it." "He subjected it against them for seven nights and eight days, in succession," [[Surat al-Haqqa: 7.]] that is, continuously. It left none of ʿAd alive except that they perished.

Hud (peace be upon him) and the believers with him withdrew into an enclosure where nothing afflicted them of that wind except what soothed the skins and delighted the souls. Indeed, it lifted up ʿAd and their households between heaven and earth and dashed them down with stones.

The delegation of ʿAd went out from Mecca until they passed by Muʿawiya ibn Bakr and stayed with him. While they were with him, a man came riding his camel on a moonlit night on the third evening after the calamity of ʿAd, and informed them of the news. They said to him: "Where did you leave Hud and his companions?" He said: "I left them at the shore of the sea," and it seems they doubted what he had told them. Hudhayla bint Bakr said:

"He has spoken truly, by the Lord of Mecca."

It is related that Marthad ibn Saʿd and Luqman ibn ʿAd, and it is said Qayl ibn ʿUnuz, when they supplicated in Mecca, were told: "You have been given your wishes; choose for yourselves, except that there is no way to immortality and death is inevitable." Mahd said: "O Allah, grant me righteousness and truthfulness," and it was granted. Luqman said: "Give me, O Lord, a lifespan," and it was said to him: "Choose for yourself the survival of seven she-goats, dark-coated, stubborn, in a rugged mountain that the rain does not touch, or the survival of seven vultures, when one vulture dies another comes after it." He chose seven vultures, and Luqman lived the lifespan of seven vultures: he would take the chick as soon as it hatched from its egg, and take the male of it for its sustenance, until it died, and then he would take another. He continued doing this until the seventh, and each vulture lived two hundred years, and the last of them was Labad. When Labad died, Luqman died with him.

As for Qayl, he chose that what had befallen his people should befall him too. It was said to him: "It is destruction," and he said: "I do not mind; I have no need of life after them," and what had befallen ʿAd of punishment befell him, and he perished. [[In full in the tafsir of al-Tabari: 8/282, no. 11493.]]

It is related from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: Allah revealed to the barren wind that it should go out against the people of ʿAd and take vengeance for Him upon them. It went out without measure, in the size of an ox's nostril, until the earth quaked from east to west. The treasurers said: "O Lord, we cannot withstand it; if it went out in its own state, it would destroy everything between the eastern and western ends of the earth." Allah revealed to it: "Return, and go out in the size of a ring's hole." So it returned and went out in the size of a ring's hole, and that is its creation. [[al-Durr al-Manthur: 3/96.]]

It is related from ʿAsim ibn ʿAmr and al-Bajali, from Abu Umama al-Bahili, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "A people of this community will spend the night over food, drink and frivolity, and in the morning they will be apes and swine, and a sinking and a stoning will befall them, and they will say: 'Last night so-and-so's house sank, and last night the house of so-and-so sank.' And the barren wind that destroyed ʿAd will surely be sent upon them, because of their drinking of wine, their consuming of usury, their taking of singing girls, their wearing of silk and their severing of the ties of kinship." [188] [[Tarikh Dimashq: 25/284.]]

And in a report: Of the wind there was sent upon them only the amount that flows through a ring. Al-Suddi said: Allah sent to ʿAd the barren wind. When it drew near them, they saw camels and men being carried through the air by the wind between heaven and earth. When they saw it, they hastened into their houses. When they entered the houses, it entered upon them and destroyed them within, then brought them out from the houses. When Allah had destroyed them, He sent upon them black birds which picked them up and cast them into the sea. No wind ever went out except by measure, except on that day; it rebelled against the treasurers and overturned them, so they did not know how much its measure was.

Abu al-Tufayl ʿAmir ibn Wathila said: I heard ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah honour his face, say to a man from Hadramawt: "Did you see a red sandhill mixed with red clay and abundant lote trees in such-and-such a region of Hadramawt?" He said: "Yes, O Commander of the Faithful. By Allah, you describe it as one who has seen it." He said: "But I have only heard of it." The Hadrami said: "What is its matter, O Commander of the Faithful?" He said: "In it is the grave of Hud, peace be upon him." [[al-Mustadrak: 2/564.]]

ʿAta ibn al-Sa'ib, from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, said: Between the Corner and the Station and Zamzam is the grave of ninety-nine prophets, and the graves of Hud, Shu'ayb, Salih and Isma'il are in that place.

In another narration: Whenever a prophet's people perished and he and the righteous with him were saved, he would go with those who were with him to Mecca, and they would worship Allah there until they died.

He continued doing this until the seventh, and each vulture lived two hundred years, and the last of them was Labad. When Labad died, Luqman died with him.

As for Qayl, he chose that what had befallen his people should befall him too. It was said to him: "It is destruction," and he said: "I do not mind; I have no need of life after them," and what had befallen ʿAd of punishment befell him, and he perished. [[In full in the tafsir of al-Tabari: 8/282, no. 11493.]]

It is related from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: Allah revealed to the barren wind that it should go out against the people of ʿAd and take vengeance for Him upon them. It went out without measure, in the size of an ox's nostril, until the earth quaked from east to west. The treasurers said: "O Lord, we cannot withstand it; if it went out in its own state, it would destroy everything between the eastern and western ends of the earth." Allah revealed to it: "Return, and go out in the size of a ring's hole." So it returned and went out in the size of a ring's hole, and that is its creation. [[al-Durr al-Manthur: 3/96.]]

It is related from ʿAsim ibn ʿAmr and al-Bajali, from Abu Umama al-Bahili, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "A people of this community will spend the night over food, drink and frivolity, and in the morning they will be apes and swine, and a sinking and a stoning will befall them, and they will say: 'Last night so-and-so's house sank, and last night the house of so-and-so sank.' And the barren wind that destroyed ʿAd will surely be sent upon them, because of their drinking of wine, their consuming of usury, their taking of singing girls, their wearing of silk and their severing of the ties of kinship." [188] [[Tarikh Dimashq: 25/284.]]

And in a report: Of the wind there was sent upon them only the amount that flows through a ring. Al-Suddi said: Allah sent to ʿAd the barren wind. When it drew near them, they saw camels and men being carried through the air by the wind between heaven and earth. When they saw it, they hastened into their houses. When they entered the houses, it entered upon them and destroyed them within, then brought them out from the houses. When Allah had destroyed them, He sent upon them black birds which picked them up and cast them into the sea. No wind ever went out except by measure, except on that day; it rebelled against the treasurers and overturned them, so they did not know how much its measure was.

Abu al-Tufayl ʿAmir ibn Wathila said: I heard ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah honour his face, say to a man from Hadramawt: "Did you see a red sandhill mixed with red clay and abundant lote trees in such-and-such a region of Hadramawt?" He said: "Yes, O Commander of the Faithful. By Allah, you describe it as one who has seen it." He said: "But I have only heard of it." The Hadrami said: "What is its matter, O Commander of the Faithful?" He said: "In it is the grave of Hud, peace be upon him." [[al-Mustadrak: 2/564.]]

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 7, verse 65–72:

[He was] their brother by lineage, not in religion: Hud, who was Hud ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Riyah ibn al-Khulud ibn ʿAd ibn ʿAwṣ ibn Adam ibn Sam ibn Nuh. Ibn Ishaq said: Hud ibn [Shalikh] ibn Arfakhshad ibn Sam ibn Nuh. He said to them: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. Will you not fear Allah?" meaning, that you single Him out and worship Him. He said: "O my people, there is no folly in me, but I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds. Al-Kalbi said: I was among you before this [day], trustworthy. "Are you amazed that a reminder from your Lord has come to you through a man from among you," meaning himself, "to warn you? Abu Hamza al-Thumali: seventy cubits. Ibn ʿAbbas: eighty. Wahb: the head of one of them was like a great dome, and a man's eye would be a nest in which beasts bred, and likewise their nostrils. See Zad al-Masir: 3/151.]] "Do you dispute with me concerning names you have named, which you have set upon idols [ ... ] [[Illegible word.]] worshipping fire, you and your fathers before you? The account of ʿAd and their destruction, as related by Muhammad ibn Ishaq, al-Suddi and others of the narrators and exegetes, is that ʿAd dwelt in Yemen, and their dwellings were there at al-Shajara and al-Ahqaf, which are sands called the sands of ʿAlij, and Dumma and Birin [[Birin: a village of Homs; Dumma: a village below al-Anbar on the Euphrates.]], between ʿUman and Hadramawt. Along with that they had spread throughout the land, subdued it and oppressed its people by virtue of the strength that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, had given them. They were worshippers of idols besides Allah: an idol called Sana, an idol called Samud, and an idol called al-Hubar.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent to them Hud as a prophet. He was of the most noble of them in lineage and the most excellent of them in descent. He commanded them to single out Allah and not to associate with Him any other god, and to refrain from wronging people, [and he did not] command them, as is related, to anything other than that.

But they refused him and denied him, and they said: "Who is mightier than us in strength?" They built monuments and seized by force like tyrants, as Allah the Exalted mentioned. When they did that, Allah withheld the rain from them for three years, until it afflicted them severely.

In that era, when calamity or war befell people, they would call upon Allah for relief and seek Allah's help at the Sacred House in Mecca, Muslim and polytheist alike. Many diverse peoples of differing religions would gather in Mecca, and all of them held Mecca in reverence, knowing its sanctity and its standing with Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The people of Mecca at that time were the Amaliq; they were called Amaliq because their father was ʿAmliq ibn Lawdh ibn Sam ibn Nuh. The chief of the Amaliq in Mecca at that time was a man called Muʿawiya ibn Bakr, and the mother of Muʿawiya was Kalhada, daughter of [al-Khaybari], a man from the Greater ʿAd. When the rain was withheld from ʿAd and they were stricken, he said: "Prepare a delegation to [seek rain] for you." They sent Qayl ibn ʿUnuz, Laqim ibn Hazal, ʿUtayl ibn Dadd ibn ʿAd the Greater, and Marthad ibn Saʿd ibn ʿUqayr.

Marthad was a Muslim who concealed his Islam, and Jalhama ibn al-Khaybari [was also there]. Muʿawiya ibn Bakra said: Then they sent Luqman ibn ʿAd ibn Sad ibn ʿAd the Greater. Each man of these people set out with a group from his people, until they reached a number [and he counted them] of seventy men. When they came to Mecca, they stayed with Muʿawiya ibn Bakr, who was outside Mecca, outside the sacred precinct. He lodged them and honored them, for they were his brothers and in-laws. They stayed with him a month drinking wine, while two singing girls belonging to Muʿawiya ibn Bakr, called al-Jaradatan, sang to them. Their journey had been a month and their stay a month. When Muʿawiya ibn Bakr saw how long they stayed, though their people had sent them seeking relief from the calamity that had befallen them, he pitied them for it and said: "My brothers and in-laws have perished, and these stay with me as my guests. By Allah, I do not know how to deal with them. I am ashamed to order them to leave for what they were sent for, lest they think I am weary of their staying with me. And those behind them among their people have perished from drought and thirst." He complained of their situation to his two singing girls, the Jaradatan, and they said: "Compose a poem that we may sing, which they will not know who said it; perhaps that will stir them."

Muʿawiya ibn Bakr said:

Perhaps Allah will give us rain as clouds... Oh Qayl, woe to you, rise and make supplication.

They have become unable to speak... so let Him water the land of ʿAd, for ʿAd...

From the fierce thirst; there is no hope for us... neither the aged shaykh nor the youth.

Their women have become sick... and their women were in good state.

The wild beasts come to them openly... and no shafts fear for ʿAd.

You are here, in what you desire... your day and your night are complete.

Wretched is your delegation from a people... they neither greet nor give salutation.

When he had recited the poem, the two singing girls sang it to them. When the people heard it, some said to others: "Your people sent you only seeking relief from you from this calamity that has descended upon them, and you have delayed too long. Enter this sanctuary and ask for water for your people." Marthad ibn Saʿd ibn ʿUqayr said: "By Allah, you will not be watered by your supplications, but if you obey your prophet and turn in repentance to Him, you will be watered." He then openly declared his Islam. Jalhama ibn [al-Khaybari], the maternal uncle of Muʿawiya, when he heard his words and knew that he had followed the religion of Hud (peace be upon him), said:

Men of nobility, and your mother is from Thamud... O Abu Saʿd, you are from a tribe...

We will not obey you as long as we live... nor will we do what you wish.

Do you order us to abandon the religion of Rifd... and the sands of al-Sada with the Samud?

Men of opinion, and we follow the religion of Hud... and abandon the religion of noble fathers.

Then he said to Muʿawiya ibn Bakr and his father Bakr, who was an old shaykh: "Detain Marthad ibn Saʿd from us, so that he does not enter Mecca with us, for he has followed the religion of Hud and abandoned our religion."

Then they set out to Mecca to seek rain for ʿAd. When they turned toward Mecca, Marthad ibn Saʿd went out from the dwelling of Muʿawiya and caught up with them there, saying: "I will not supplicate Allah, Mighty and Majestic, for anything they set out for." When he reached them, he stood to supplicate Allah while they had gathered to call upon Allah, and he said: "O Allah, grant me my request alone, and do not include me in anything they ask of You." Qayl ibn ʿUnuz was at the head of the delegation of ʿAd, and the delegation of ʿAd said: "O Allah, grant him what he asks of You and make our request together with his request." He had [stayed behind] from the delegation of ʿAd when Luqman ibn ʿAd prayed, and he was the chief of ʿAd. When they had finished their supplication, he stood and said: "O Allah, I have come to You alone in my need, so grant me my request," and he asked Allah, Mighty and Majestic, for long life. He was granted the lifespan of seven vultures. Qayl ibn ʿUnuz said: "[O our God], if Hud is truthful, give us rain, for we are destroyed."

He said: "O Allah, I did not come for a sick man that I might treat him, nor for a captive that I might call to him. O Allah, water ʿAd with what You used to water them." Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, produced for him [clouds] of three kinds: white, red and black. Then a caller called from heaven: "O Qayl, choose for yourself and your people from this cloud whatever you wish." Qayl said: "I have chosen the black cloud, for it is the largest of clouds." The caller called to him: "You have chosen a whirlwind of ashes, dust upon dust, that will leave none of ʿAd, neither parent nor child, but will make them all ruins, except the sons of al-Luwdhiyya al-Muhdha."

The sons of al-Luwdhiyya are the sons of Luqaym ibn Hazal ibn Hazayla ibn Bakr. They were residents of Mecca with their maternal uncles, and they were not with ʿAd in their land. The other ʿAd were from the offspring of those of ʿAd who survived.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent forth the black cloud that Qayl had chosen, [containing vengeance] upon ʿAd, until it came out upon them from a valley of theirs called al-Mughith. When they saw it they rejoiced, and said: "This is a cloud bringing us rain." Allah the Exalted says: "Rather, it is that which you sought to hasten: a wind wherein is a painful punishment, destroying everything by the command of its Lord." [[Surat al-Ahqaf: 24–25.]]

The first to perceive what was in it and to recognise that it was a wind was a woman of ʿAd called Mahdar. When it came upon them, she cried out and fell unconscious. When she recovered, they said: "What did you see?" She said: "I saw its wind, and in it were sparks like fire, and before it were men leading it." "He subjected it against them for seven nights and eight days, in succession," [[Surat al-Haqqa: 7.]] that is, continuously. It left none of ʿAd alive except that they perished.

Hud (peace be upon him) and the believers with him withdrew into an enclosure where nothing afflicted them of that wind except what soothed the skins and delighted the souls. Indeed, it lifted up ʿAd and their households between heaven and earth and dashed them down with stones.

The delegation of ʿAd went out from Mecca until they passed by Muʿawiya ibn Bakr and stayed with him. While they were with him, a man came riding his camel on a moonlit night on the third evening after the calamity of ʿAd, and informed them of the news. They said to him: "Where did you leave Hud and his companions?" He said: "I left them at the shore of the sea," and it seems they doubted what he had told them. Hudhayla bint Bakr said:

"He has spoken truly, by the Lord of Mecca."

Marthad ibn Saʿd ibn ʿUqayr said: "By Allah, you will not be watered by your supplications, but if you obey your prophet and turn in repentance to Him, you will be watered." He then openly declared his Islam. Jalhama ibn [al-Khaybari], the maternal uncle of Muʿawiya, when he heard his words and knew that he had followed the religion of Hud (peace be upon him), said:

Men of nobility, and your mother is from Thamud... O Abu Saʿd, you are from a tribe...

We will not obey you as long as we live... nor will we do what you wish.

Do you order us to abandon the religion of Rifd... and the sands of al-Sada with the Samud?

Men of opinion, and we follow the religion of Hud... and abandon the religion of noble fathers.

Then he said to Muʿawiya ibn Bakr and his father Bakr, who was an old shaykh: "Detain Marthad ibn Saʿd from us, so that he does not enter Mecca with us, for he has followed the religion of Hud and abandoned our religion."

Then they set out to Mecca to seek rain for ʿAd. When they turned toward Mecca, Marthad ibn Saʿd went out from the dwelling of Muʿawiya and caught up with them there, saying: "I will not supplicate Allah, Mighty and Majestic, for anything they set out for." When he reached them, he stood to supplicate Allah while they had gathered to call upon Allah, and he said: "O Allah, grant me my request alone, and do not include me in anything they ask of You." Qayl ibn ʿUnuz was at the head of the delegation of ʿAd, and the delegation of ʿAd said: "O Allah, grant him what he asks of You and make our request together with his request." He had [stayed behind] from the delegation of ʿAd when Luqman ibn ʿAd prayed, and he was the chief of ʿAd. When they had finished their supplication, he stood and said: "O Allah, I have come to You alone in my need, so grant me my request," and he asked Allah, Mighty and Majestic, for long life. He was granted the lifespan of seven vultures. Qayl ibn ʿUnuz said: "[O our God], if Hud is truthful, give us rain, for we are destroyed."

He said: "O Allah, I did not come for a sick man that I might treat him, nor for a captive that I might call to him. O Allah, water ʿAd with what You used to water them." Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, produced for him [clouds] of three kinds: white, red and black. Then a caller called from heaven: "O Qayl, choose for yourself and your people from this cloud whatever you wish." Qayl said: "I have chosen the black cloud, for it is the largest of clouds." The caller called to him: "You have chosen a whirlwind of ashes, dust upon dust, that will leave none of ʿAd, neither parent nor child, but will make them all ruins, except the sons of al-Luwdhiyya al-Muhdha."

The sons of al-Luwdhiyya are the sons of Luqaym ibn Hazal ibn Hazayla ibn Bakr. They were residents of Mecca with their maternal uncles, and they were not with ʿAd in their land. The other ʿAd were from the offspring of those of ʿAd who survived.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent forth the black cloud that Qayl had chosen, [containing vengeance] upon ʿAd, until it came out upon them from a valley of theirs called al-Mughith. When they saw it they rejoiced, and said: "This is a cloud bringing us rain." Allah the Exalted says: "Rather, it is that which you sought to hasten: a wind wherein is a painful punishment, destroying everything by the command of its Lord." [[Surat al-Ahqaf: 24–25.]]

The first to perceive what was in it and to recognise that it was a wind was a woman of ʿAd called Mahdar. When it came upon them, she cried out and fell unconscious. When she recovered, they said: "What did you see?" She said: "I saw its wind, and in it were sparks like fire, and before it were men leading it." "He subjected it against them for seven nights and eight days, in succession," [[Surat al-Haqqa: 7.]] that is, continuously. It left none of ʿAd alive except that they perished.

Hud (peace be upon him) and the believers with him withdrew into an enclosure where nothing afflicted them of that wind except what soothed the skins and delighted the souls. Indeed, it lifted up ʿAd and their households between heaven and earth and dashed them down with stones.

The delegation of ʿAd went out from Mecca until they passed by Muʿawiya ibn Bakr and stayed with him. While they were with him, a man came riding his camel on a moonlit night on the third evening after the calamity of ʿAd, and informed them of the news. They said to him: "Where did you leave Hud and his companions?" He said: "I left them at the shore of the sea," and it seems they doubted what he had told them. Hudhayla bint Bakr said:

"He has spoken truly, by the Lord of Mecca."

It is related that Marthad ibn Saʿd and Luqman ibn ʿAd, and it is said Qayl ibn ʿUnuz, when they supplicated in Mecca, were told: "You have been given your wishes; choose for yourselves, except that there is no way to immortality and death is inevitable." Mahd said: "O Allah, grant me righteousness and truthfulness," and it was granted. Luqman said: "Give me, O Lord, a lifespan," and it was said to him: "Choose for yourself the survival of seven she-goats, dark-coated, stubborn, in a rugged mountain that the rain does not touch, or the survival of seven vultures, when one vulture dies another comes after it." He chose seven vultures, and Luqman lived the lifespan of seven vultures: he would take the chick as soon as it hatched from its egg, and take the male of it for its sustenance, until it died, and then he would take another. He continued doing this until the seventh, and each vulture lived two hundred years, and the last of them was Labad. When Labad died, Luqman died with him.

As for Qayl, he chose that what had befallen his people should befall him too. It was said to him: "It is destruction," and he said: "I do not mind; I have no need of life after them," and what had befallen ʿAd of punishment befell him, and he perished. [[In full in the tafsir of al-Tabari: 8/282, no. 11493.]]

It is related from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: Allah revealed to the barren wind that it should go out against the people of ʿAd and take vengeance for Him upon them. It went out without measure, in the size of an ox's nostril, until the earth quaked from east to west. The treasurers said: "O Lord, we cannot withstand it; if it went out in its own state, it would destroy everything between the eastern and western ends of the earth." Allah revealed to it: "Return, and go out in the size of a ring's hole." So it returned and went out in the size of a ring's hole, and that is its creation. [[al-Durr al-Manthur: 3/96.]]

It is related from ʿAsim ibn ʿAmr and al-Bajali, from Abu Umama al-Bahili, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "A people of this community will spend the night over food, drink and frivolity, and in the morning they will be apes and swine, and a sinking and a stoning will befall them, and they will say: 'Last night so-and-so's house sank, and last night the house of so-and-so sank.' And the barren wind that destroyed ʿAd will surely be sent upon them, because of their drinking of wine, their consuming of usury, their taking of singing girls, their wearing of silk and their severing of the ties of kinship." [188] [[Tarikh Dimashq: 25/284.]]

And in a report: Of the wind there was sent upon them only the amount that flows through a ring. Al-Suddi said: Allah sent to ʿAd the barren wind. When it drew near them, they saw camels and men being carried through the air by the wind between heaven and earth. When they saw it, they hastened into their houses. When they entered the houses, it entered upon them and destroyed them within, then brought them out from the houses. When Allah had destroyed them, He sent upon them black birds which picked them up and cast them into the sea. No wind ever went out except by measure, except on that day; it rebelled against the treasurers and overturned them, so they did not know how much its measure was.

Abu al-Tufayl ʿAmir ibn Wathila said: I heard ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah honour his face, say to a man from Hadramawt: "Did you see a red sandhill mixed with red clay and abundant lote trees in such-and-such a region of Hadramawt?" He said: "Yes, O Commander of the Faithful. By Allah, you describe it as one who has seen it." He said: "But I have only heard of it." The Hadrami said: "What is its matter, O Commander of the Faithful?" He said: "In it is the grave of Hud, peace be upon him." [[al-Mustadrak: 2/564.]]

ʿAta ibn al-Sa'ib, from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, said: Between the Corner and the Station and Zamzam is the grave of ninety-nine prophets, and the graves of Hud, Shu'ayb, Salih and Isma'il are in that place.

In another narration: Whenever a prophet's people perished and he and the righteous with him were saved, he would go with those who were with him to Mecca, and they would worship Allah there until they died.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 7, verse 65–72:

And to ʿAd [We sent] their brother Hud. Meaning: We sent to ʿAd, hence the accusative in "akhahum" (their brother). He was ʿAlaʾ ibn ʿAwṣ ibn Adam ibn Sam ibn Nuh, and he is the first ʿAd. [He was] their brother by lineage, not in religion: Hud, who was Hud ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Riyah ibn al-Khulud ibn ʿAd ibn ʿAwṣ ibn Adam ibn Sam ibn Nuh. Ibn Ishaq said: Hud ibn [Shalikh] ibn Arfakhshad ibn Sam ibn Nuh. He said to them: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. He said: "O my people, there is no folly in me, but I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds. Abu Hamza al-Thumali: seventy cubits. Ibn ʿAbbas: eighty. Wahb: the head of one of them was like a great dome, and a man's eye would be a nest in which beasts bred, and likewise their nostrils. See Zad al-Masir: 3/151.]] "Do you dispute with me concerning names you have named, which you have set upon idols [ ... ] [[Illegible word.]] worshipping fire, you and your fathers before you? Allah has sent down no authority for them," no proof, clarification or evidence. "So wait; I am with you among those who wait." Then We saved him, meaning Hud, at the descent of the punishment.

"And those with him by a mercy from Us, and We cut off the root of those who denied Our signs," that is, We uprooted them and destroyed them entirely, "and they were not believers."

The account of ʿAd and their destruction, as related by Muhammad ibn Ishaq, al-Suddi and others of the narrators and exegetes, is that ʿAd dwelt in Yemen, and their dwellings were there at al-Shajara and al-Ahqaf, which are sands called the sands of ʿAlij, and Dumma and Birin [[Birin: a village of Homs; Dumma: a village below al-Anbar on the Euphrates.]], between ʿUman and Hadramawt. Along with that they had spread throughout the land, subdued it and oppressed its people by virtue of the strength that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, had given them. They were worshippers of idols besides Allah: an idol called Sana, an idol called Samud, and an idol called al-Hubar.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent to them Hud as a prophet. He was of the most noble of them in lineage and the most excellent of them in descent. He commanded them to single out Allah and not to associate with Him any other god, and to refrain from wronging people, [and he did not] command them, as is related, to anything other than that.

But they refused him and denied him, and they said: "Who is mightier than us in strength?" They built monuments and seized by force like tyrants, as Allah the Exalted mentioned. When they did that, Allah withheld the rain from them for three years, until it afflicted them severely.

In that era, when calamity or war befell people, they would call upon Allah for relief and seek Allah's help at the Sacred House in Mecca, Muslim and polytheist alike. Many diverse peoples of differing religions would gather in Mecca, and all of them held Mecca in reverence, knowing its sanctity and its standing with Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The people of Mecca at that time were the Amaliq; they were called Amaliq because their father was ʿAmliq ibn Lawdh ibn Sam ibn Nuh. The chief of the Amaliq in Mecca at that time was a man called Muʿawiya ibn Bakr, and the mother of Muʿawiya was Kalhada, daughter of [al-Khaybari], a man from the Greater ʿAd. When the rain was withheld from ʿAd and they were stricken, he said: "Prepare a delegation to [seek rain] for you." They sent Qayl ibn ʿUnuz, Laqim ibn Hazal, ʿUtayl ibn Dadd ibn ʿAd the Greater, and Marthad ibn Saʿd ibn ʿUqayr.

Marthad was a Muslim who concealed his Islam, and Jalhama ibn al-Khaybari [was also there]. Muʿawiya ibn Bakra said: Then they sent Luqman ibn ʿAd ibn Sad ibn ʿAd the Greater. Each man of these people set out with a group from his people, until they reached a number [and he counted them] of seventy men. When they came to Mecca, they stayed with Muʿawiya ibn Bakr, who was outside Mecca, outside the sacred precinct. He lodged them and honored them, for they were his brothers and in-laws. They stayed with him a month drinking wine, while two singing girls belonging to Muʿawiya ibn Bakr, called al-Jaradatan, sang to them. Their journey had been a month and their stay a month. When Muʿawiya ibn Bakr saw how long they stayed, though their people had sent them seeking relief from the calamity that had befallen them, he pitied them for it and said: "My brothers and in-laws have perished, and these stay with me as my guests. By Allah, I do not know how to deal with them. I am ashamed to order them to leave for what they were sent for, lest they think I am weary of their staying with me. And those behind them among their people have perished from drought and thirst." He complained of their situation to his two singing girls, the Jaradatan, and they said: "Compose a poem that we may sing, which they will not know who said it; perhaps that will stir them."

Muʿawiya ibn Bakr said:

Perhaps Allah will give us rain as clouds... Oh Qayl, woe to you, rise and make supplication.

They have become unable to speak... so let Him water the land of ʿAd, for ʿAd...

From the fierce thirst; there is no hope for us... neither the aged shaykh nor the youth.

Their women have become sick... and their women were in good state.

The wild beasts come to them openly... and no shafts fear for ʿAd.

You are here, in what you desire... your day and your night are complete.

Wretched is your delegation from a people... they neither greet nor give salutation.

When he had recited the poem, the two singing girls sang it to them. When the people heard it, some said to others: "Your people sent you only seeking relief from you from this calamity that has descended upon them, and you have delayed too long. "And those with him by a mercy from Us, and We cut off the root of those who denied Our signs," that is, We uprooted them and destroyed them entirely, "and they were not believers."

The account of ʿAd and their destruction, as related by Muhammad ibn Ishaq, al-Suddi and others of the narrators and exegetes, is that ʿAd dwelt in Yemen, and their dwellings were there at al-Shajara and al-Ahqaf, which are sands called the sands of ʿAlij, and Dumma and Birin [[Birin: a village of Homs; Dumma: a village below al-Anbar on the Euphrates.]], between ʿUman and Hadramawt. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent to them Hud as a prophet. He was of the most noble of them in lineage and the most excellent of them in descent. He commanded them to single out Allah and not to associate with Him any other god, and to refrain from wronging people, [and he did not] command them, as is related, to anything other than that.

But they refused him and denied him, and they said: "Who is mightier than us in strength?" They built monuments and seized by force like tyrants, as Allah the Exalted mentioned. When they did that, Allah withheld the rain from them for three years, until it afflicted them severely.

In that era, when calamity or war befell people, they would call upon Allah for relief and seek Allah's help at the Sacred House in Mecca, Muslim and polytheist alike. Many diverse peoples of differing religions would gather in Mecca, and all of them held Mecca in reverence, knowing its sanctity and its standing with Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The people of Mecca at that time were the Amaliq; they were called Amaliq because their father was ʿAmliq ibn Lawdh ibn Sam ibn Nuh. The chief of the Amaliq in Mecca at that time was a man called Muʿawiya ibn Bakr, and the mother of Muʿawiya was Kalhada, daughter of [al-Khaybari], a man from the Greater ʿAd. When the rain was withheld from ʿAd and they were stricken, he said: "Prepare a delegation to [seek rain] for you." They sent Qayl ibn ʿUnuz, Laqim ibn Hazal, ʿUtayl ibn Dadd ibn ʿAd the Greater, and Marthad ibn Saʿd ibn ʿUqayr.

Marthad was a Muslim who concealed his Islam, and Jalhama ibn al-Khaybari [was also there]. Muʿawiya ibn Bakra said: Then they sent Luqman ibn ʿAd ibn Sad ibn ʿAd the Greater. Each man of these people set out with a group from his people, until they reached a number [and he counted them] of seventy men. When they came to Mecca, they stayed with Muʿawiya ibn Bakr, who was outside Mecca, outside the sacred precinct. He lodged them and honored them, for they were his brothers and in-laws. They stayed with him a month drinking wine, while two singing girls belonging to Muʿawiya ibn Bakr, called al-Jaradatan, sang to them. Their journey had been a month and their stay a month. When Muʿawiya ibn Bakr saw how long they stayed, though their people had sent them seeking relief from the calamity that had befallen them, he pitied them for it and said: "My brothers and in-laws have perished, and these stay with me as my guests. By Allah, I do not know how to deal with them. I am ashamed to order them to leave for what they were sent for, lest they think I am weary of their staying with me. And those behind them among their people have perished from drought and thirst." He complained of their situation to his two singing girls, the Jaradatan, and they said: "Compose a poem that we may sing, which they will not know who said it; perhaps that will stir them."

Muʿawiya ibn Bakr said:

Perhaps Allah will give us rain as clouds... Oh Qayl, woe to you, rise and make supplication.

They have become unable to speak... so let Him water the land of ʿAd, for ʿAd...

From the fierce thirst; there is no hope for us... neither the aged shaykh nor the youth.

Their women have become sick... and their women were in good state.

The wild beasts come to them openly... and no shafts fear for ʿAd.

You are here, in what you desire... your day and your night are complete.

Wretched is your delegation from a people... they neither greet nor give salutation.

When he had recited the poem, the two singing girls sang it to them. When the people heard it, some said to others: "Your people sent you only seeking relief from you from this calamity that has descended upon them, and you have delayed too long. Enter this sanctuary and ask for water for your people." Marthad ibn Saʿd ibn ʿUqayr said: "By Allah, you will not be watered by your supplications, but if you obey your prophet and turn in repentance to Him, you will be watered." He then openly declared his Islam. Jalhama ibn [al-Khaybari], the maternal uncle of Muʿawiya, when he heard his words and knew that he had followed the religion of Hud (peace be upon him), said:

Men of nobility, and your mother is from Thamud... O Abu Saʿd, you are from a tribe...

We will not obey you as long as we live... nor will we do what you wish.

Do you order us to abandon the religion of Rifd... and the sands of al-Sada with the Samud?

Men of opinion, and we follow the religion of Hud... and abandon the religion of noble fathers.

Then he said to Muʿawiya ibn Bakr and his father Bakr, who was an old shaykh: "Detain Marthad ibn Saʿd from us, so that he does not enter Mecca with us, for he has followed the religion of Hud and abandoned our religion."

Then they set out to Mecca to seek rain for ʿAd. When they turned toward Mecca, Marthad ibn Saʿd went out from the dwelling of Muʿawiya and caught up with them there, saying: "I will not supplicate Allah, Mighty and Majestic, for anything they set out for." When he reached them, he stood to supplicate Allah while they had gathered to call upon Allah, and he said: "O Allah, grant me my request alone, and do not include me in anything they ask of You." Qayl ibn ʿUnuz was at the head of the delegation of ʿAd, and the delegation of ʿAd said: "O Allah, grant him what he asks of You and make our request together with his request." He had [stayed behind] from the delegation of ʿAd when Luqman ibn ʿAd prayed, and he was the chief of ʿAd. When they had finished their supplication, he stood and said: "O Allah, I have come to You alone in my need, so grant me my request," and he asked Allah, Mighty and Majestic, for long life. He was granted the lifespan of seven vultures. Qayl ibn ʿUnuz said: "[O our God], if Hud is truthful, give us rain, for we are destroyed."

He said: "O Allah, I did not come for a sick man that I might treat him, nor for a captive that I might call to him. O Allah, water ʿAd with what You used to water them." Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, produced for him [clouds] of three kinds: white, red and black. Then a caller called from heaven: "O Qayl, choose for yourself and your people from this cloud whatever you wish." Qayl said: "I have chosen the black cloud, for it is the largest of clouds." The caller called to him: "You have chosen a whirlwind of ashes, dust upon dust, that will leave none of ʿAd, neither parent nor child, but will make them all ruins, except the sons of al-Luwdhiyya al-Muhdha."

The sons of al-Luwdhiyya are the sons of Luqaym ibn Hazal ibn Hazayla ibn Bakr. They were residents of Mecca with their maternal uncles, and they were not with ʿAd in their land. The other ʿAd were from the offspring of those of ʿAd who survived.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent forth the black cloud that Qayl had chosen, [containing vengeance] upon ʿAd, until it came out upon them from a valley of theirs called al-Mughith. When they saw it they rejoiced, and said: "This is a cloud bringing us rain." Allah the Exalted says: "Rather, it is that which you sought to hasten: a wind wherein is a painful punishment, destroying everything by the command of its Lord." [[Surat al-Ahqaf: 24–25.]]

The first to perceive what was in it and to recognise that it was a wind was a woman of ʿAd called Mahdar. When it came upon them, she cried out and fell unconscious. When she recovered, they said: "What did you see?" She said: "I saw its wind, and in it were sparks like fire, and before it were men leading it." "He subjected it against them for seven nights and eight days, in succession," [[Surat al-Haqqa: 7.]] that is, continuously. It left none of ʿAd alive except that they perished.

Hud (peace be upon him) and the believers with him withdrew into an enclosure where nothing afflicted them of that wind except what soothed the skins and delighted the souls. Indeed, it lifted up ʿAd and their households between heaven and earth and dashed them down with stones.

The delegation of ʿAd went out from Mecca until they passed by Muʿawiya ibn Bakr and stayed with him. While they were with him, a man came riding his camel on a moonlit night on the third evening after the calamity of ʿAd, and informed them of the news. They said to him: "Where did you leave Hud and his companions?" He said: "I left them at the shore of the sea," and it seems they doubted what he had told them. Hudhayla bint Bakr said:

"He has spoken truly, by the Lord of Mecca."

It is related that Marthad ibn Saʿd and Luqman ibn ʿAd, and it is said Qayl ibn ʿUnuz, when they supplicated in Mecca, were told: "You have been given your wishes; choose for yourselves, except that there is no way to immortality and death is inevitable." Mahd said: "O Allah, grant me righteousness and truthfulness," and it was granted. Luqman said: "Give me, O Lord, a lifespan," and it was said to him: "Choose for yourself the survival of seven she-goats, dark-coated, stubborn, in a rugged mountain that the rain does not touch, or the survival of seven vultures, when one vulture dies another comes after it." He chose seven vultures, and Luqman lived the lifespan of seven vultures: he would take the chick as soon as it hatched from its egg, and take the male of it for its sustenance, until it died, and then he would take another. He continued doing this until the seventh, and each vulture lived two hundred years, and the last of them was Labad. When Labad died, Luqman died with him.

As for Qayl, he chose that what had befallen his people should befall him too. It was said to him: "It is destruction," and he said: "I do not mind; I have no need of life after them," and what had befallen ʿAd of punishment befell him, and he perished. [[In full in the tafsir of al-Tabari: 8/282, no. 11493.]]

It is related from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: Allah revealed to the barren wind that it should go out against the people of ʿAd and take vengeance for Him upon them. It went out without measure, in the size of an ox's nostril, until the earth quaked from east to west. The treasurers said: "O Lord, we cannot withstand it; if it went out in its own state, it would destroy everything between the eastern and western ends of the earth." Allah revealed to it: "Return, and go out in the size of a ring's hole." So it returned and went out in the size of a ring's hole, and that is its creation. [[al-Durr al-Manthur: 3/96.]]

It is related from ʿAsim ibn ʿAmr and al-Bajali, from Abu Umama al-Bahili, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "A people of this community will spend the night over food, drink and frivolity, and in the morning they will be apes and swine, and a sinking and a stoning will befall them, and they will say: 'Last night so-and-so's house sank, and last night the house of so-and-so sank.' And the barren wind that destroyed ʿAd will surely be sent upon them, because of their drinking of wine, their consuming of usury, their taking of singing girls, their wearing of silk and their severing of the ties of kinship." [188] [[Tarikh Dimashq: 25/284.]]

And in a report: Of the wind there was sent upon them only the amount that flows through a ring. Al-Suddi said: Allah sent to ʿAd the barren wind. When it drew near them, they saw camels and men being carried through the air by the wind between heaven and earth. When they saw it, they hastened into their houses. When they entered the houses, it entered upon them and destroyed them within, then brought them out from the houses. When Allah had destroyed them, He sent upon them black birds which picked them up and cast them into the sea. No wind ever went out except by measure, except on that day; it rebelled against the treasurers and overturned them, so they did not know how much its measure was.

Abu al-Tufayl ʿAmir ibn Wathila said: I heard ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah honour his face, say to a man from Hadramawt: "Did you see a red sandhill mixed with red clay and abundant lote trees in such-and-such a region of Hadramawt?" He said: "Yes, O Commander of the Faithful. By Allah, you describe it as one who has seen it." He said: "But I have only heard of it." The Hadrami said: "What is its matter, O Commander of the Faithful?" He said: "In it is the grave of Hud, peace be upon him." [[al-Mustadrak: 2/564.]]

ʿAta ibn al-Sa'ib, from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, said: Between the Corner and the Station and Zamzam is the grave of ninety-nine prophets, and the graves of Hud, Shu'ayb, Salih and Isma'il are in that place.

In another narration: Whenever a prophet's people perished and he and the righteous with him were saved, he would go with those who were with him to Mecca, and they would worship Allah there until they died.

It was said to him: "It is destruction," and he said: "I do not mind; I have no need of life after them," and what had befallen ʿAd of punishment befell him, and he perished. [[In full in the tafsir of al-Tabari: 8/282, no. 11493.]]

It is related from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: Allah revealed to the barren wind that it should go out against the people of ʿAd and take vengeance for Him upon them. It went out without measure, in the size of an ox's nostril, until the earth quaked from east to west. The treasurers said: "O Lord, we cannot withstand it; if it went out in its own state, it would destroy everything between the eastern and western ends of the earth." Allah revealed to it: "Return, and go out in the size of a ring's hole." So it returned and went out in the size of a ring's hole, and that is its creation. [[al-Durr al-Manthur: 3/96.]]

It is related from ʿAsim ibn ʿAmr and al-Bajali, from Abu Umama al-Bahili, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "A people of this community will spend the night over food, drink and frivolity, and in the morning they will be apes and swine, and a sinking and a stoning will befall them, and they will say: 'Last night so-and-so's house sank, and last night the house of so-and-so sank.' And the barren wind that destroyed ʿAd will surely be sent upon them, because of their drinking of wine, their consuming of usury, their taking of singing girls, their wearing of silk and their severing of the ties of kinship." [188] [[Tarikh Dimashq: 25/284.]]

And in a report: Of the wind there was sent upon them only the amount that flows through a ring. Al-Suddi said: Allah sent to ʿAd the barren wind. When it drew near them, they saw camels and men being carried through the air by the wind between heaven and earth. When they saw it, they hastened into their houses. When they entered the houses, it entered upon them and destroyed them within, then brought them out from the houses. When Allah had destroyed them, He sent upon them black birds which picked them up and cast them into the sea. No wind ever went out except by measure, except on that day; it rebelled against the treasurers and overturned them, so they did not know how much its measure was.

Abu al-Tufayl ʿAmir ibn Wathila said: I heard ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah honour his face, say to a man from Hadramawt: "Did you see a red sandhill mixed with red clay and abundant lote trees in such-and-such a region of Hadramawt?" He said: "Yes, O Commander of the Faithful. By Allah, you describe it as one who has seen it." He said: "But I have only heard of it." The Hadrami said: "What is its matter, O Commander of the Faithful?" He said: "In it is the grave of Hud, peace be upon him." [[al-Mustadrak: 2/564.]]

ʿAta ibn al-Sa'ib, from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, said: Between the Corner and the Station and Zamzam is the grave of ninety-nine prophets, and the graves of Hud, Shu'ayb, Salih and Isma'il are in that place.

In another narration: Whenever a prophet's people perished and he and the righteous with him were saved, he would go with those who were with him to Mecca, and they would worship Allah there until they died.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 7, verse 73–79 (part 1 of 2):

And to Thamud [We sent] their brother Salih. Yahya ibn Wathhab recited: "ilā Thamūdin" with tanwin and without the diptote (ṣarf). The rest recited it without ṣarf. What is meant is: "and to the sons of Thamud," and he is Thamud ibn [Ad] ibn Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh, and he is the brother of [Jadis]. Here he intends the tribe.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala said: Thamud was named so for the scarcity of its water, for al-thamd means little water. Their dwellings were the rock-cut houses (al-Hijr) between the Hijaz and al-Sham, up to Wadi al-Qura. [They were sent to] their brother Salih, and he is Salih ibn [Ubayd] ibn Asaf ibn Masikh ibn Ubayd ibn Khadir ibn Thamud. He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. There has certainly come to you clear evidence from your Lord," meaning a proof and a sign from your Lord confirming my truthfulness. "This is the she-camel of Allah for you," He attributed it to Himself as a mark of distinction and specification, as one says "the House of Allah" [[See Tarikh al-Tabari: 1/158.]].

It was also said: she was attributed to Allah because she came into being by [Divine] creation without the union of a male and female, and she was not from a loin or a womb, and creatures had no effort in her. "A sign" is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: look at this she-camel. "Leave her to graze on Allah's earth, and do not touch her with harm, lest a painful punishment seize you." "And remember when He made you successors after 'Ad, and settled you in the land, taking from its plains palaces, and hewing the mountains into houses," [Al-Hasan recited "wa-tanḥatūna" with a fatḥa on the ḥa', which is a dialect form], and they used to carve out houses in the mountains. "So remember the favours of Allah, and do not commit corruption in the land, causing mischief."

"The chiefs of his people who were arrogant said," meaning the nobles and leaders who exalted themselves above faith in Salih (peace be upon him), "to those who were deemed weak," meaning the followers, "among those who believed: Do you know that Salih is sent from his Lord?" They said: "Indeed, we believe in what he has been sent with." Those who were arrogant said: "Indeed, we are disbelievers in that which you believe" (jāḥidūn, deniers). "Then they hamstrung the she-camel," slaughtered her, "and they rebelled against the command of their Lord, and said: O Salih, bring us what you threaten us with," meaning the punishment, "if you are one of the messengers," i.e., one of the truthful. "So the quake seized them," meaning the cry and the earthquake; its root meaning is movement with sound. Allah said: "The day the quaker quakes" [al-Nazi'at 6]. A poet said:

"When the pilgrimage's time had come, the camels of the people shook" ... 
And al-Akhtal said:
"Do you not see me, the white hair of old age has grown upon my temples; I am old like an eagle, the man shaking, weakened by it" ...
[Tafsir al-Tabari: 8/302.]

"So they became in their home," i.e., in their land and their town; that is why "home" is singular. It was also said he meant the dwellings (diyar), and used the singular as in Allah's words: "Indeed, mankind is in loss" [al-'Asr 2]. The meaning of "jathimin" is prostrate, [humbled, struck down], fallen dead; the root of al-jathim is one who sits on his knees.

Jarir said:
"You knew the place of departure and you knew from it the crouching camels like crows" ...
[Tafsir al-Tabari: 8/303.]

"Then he turned away from them," [Salih turned away from them], and said: "O my people, I certainly conveyed to you the message of my Lord and advised you, but you do not love those who give advice." The story of Salih and Thamud and their hamstringing of the she-camel was the cause of their destruction, according to what Ibn Ishaq, al-Suddi, Wahb, Ka'b and others of the People of the Book have mentioned. They said: when 'Ad were destroyed and their affair came to an end, their lifespans were lengthened and they were made successors in the land; they multiplied and prospered there, until one of them would build a dwelling of clay and it would collapse while the man was still alive. When they saw that, they took the mountains as houses, hewed them, bored them, and cut them out, and they were in ease regarding their livelihoods. Then they transgressed against Allah, committed corruption in the land, and worshipped other than Allah. So Allah sent Salih to them. They were Arabs in that place. Salih was among the most noble of them in lineage and the most excellent in standing.

Allah sent him to them while he was young; he called them to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, until he grew gray and old, and none followed him except a few weak ones. When Salih pressed them with supplication and communication, and greatly warned and frightened them, they asked him to show them a sign that would confirm his words. He said: "What sign do you want?" They said: "We want you to come out with us to this festival of ours," and the name of the festival was that they went out to it with their idols on a known day of the year: "you call on your god and we call on ours; if our call is answered, we will follow you, and if yours is answered, you will follow us."

Salih said to them: "Yes." So they went out with their idols to that festival, and Salih went out with them. They called on their idols and asked them that Salih's supplication not be answered in anything. Then Jundu' ibn 'Amr ibn Harash, who was at that time the chief of Thamud, said: "O Salih, bring forth for us from this rock," a single rock in a corner of al-Hijr called al-Katiba, "a she-camel, pregnant (mukhtarijah), hollow-bellied and free of blemish." The mukhtarijah is one resembling the bukht (Bactrian camel) among camels. "If you do it, we will believe you and we will have faith in you." Salih took their covenant that if he did it, they would truly believe him and have faith in him. They said: "Yes."

Salih prayed two rak'as and called on his Lord, and the rock writhed like a woman in labour bringing forth her child, then the hillock moved and split open, bringing forth a she-camel, ten [months pregnant], hollow-bellied and free of blemish, as they had asked. No one knows what is between her sides except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, while they watched; then she gave birth to a young one like her in size. Jundu' ibn 'Amr and a group of his people believed in him. The nobles of Thamud wanted to believe and accept him, but Dhu'ab ibn 'Amr ibn Labid, al-Habbab, the owner of their idols, and Rabab ibn Sam'ar forbade them; they were among the nobles of Thamud. Jundu' ibn 'Amr had a paternal cousin called Shihab ibn Khalifa ibn Makhlah ibn Labid, who wanted to embrace Islam, but that group forbade him and he obeyed them. A man of the family of Thamud said:

"Shihab was called to the religion of the Prophet, and a clan of the family of 'Amr was ready..."
