Sunaym said to her: "Rather, I will contend with you before the Banu Mirdas ibn 'Ubayd." That was because the Banu Mirdas were Muslims.

She said: "I will not contend with you except before whom you invited me to." The Banu Mirdas said: "By Allah, you will give him his children, unwilling or willing." When she saw that, she gave them to him.

Then Sadduf and 'Unayza plotted together to hamstring the she-camel because of the misfortune that had befallen them. Sadduf called a man of Thamud called [al-Habbab] to hamstring the she-camel and offered herself to him if he did it, but he refused her. She then called a paternal cousin of hers called Mus'ad ibn Mahraj ibn al-Muhayya, and made herself available to him on condition that he hamstring the she-camel; he was among the most handsome of people and the wealthiest, and he agreed to that. 'Unayza bint Ghanm called Qudar ibn Salif ibn Jundu' a man from the people of Qirah.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mentioned him and said: "A mighty, fierce, invincible man among his clan was dispatched for her, like Abu Zam'a." [189] [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 30/269.]] His mother's name was Qadir. He was a short, reddish-blue man; they claim he was born of fornication with a man called Sibyan, and he was not of Salif, who was called the "secret one," but he was born on Salif's bed. She said: "I will give you whichever of my daughters you wish, on condition that you hamstring the she-camel." Qudar was mighty and invincible among his people. So Qudar ibn Salif and Mus'ad ibn Mahraj set out and mobilized deviants of Thamud, and seven men followed them; they were nine men, the leader of whom was Huwayl ibn Mistah, maternal uncle of 'Aziz from the people of Hijr, [and Du'ayb] ibn Ghanm ibn Dhagir, Dhu'ab ibn Mahraj ibn Mus'ad, and five whose names were not mentioned to us. They agreed to hamstring the she-camel.

Al-Suddi and others said: Allah revealed to Salih (peace be upon him) that his people would hamstring his she-camel; he told them that. They said: "We would never do that." Salih said: "A boy will be born among your people who will hamstring her, and your destruction will be at his hands." They said: "No son will be born to us in this month except that we will kill him."

He said: "Nine were born to them in that month. They killed their children; then the tenth was born, and he refused to slaughter his son, for he had no son before that. The son of the tenth was red and blue, and grew quickly. Whenever he passed by the nine and they saw him, they said: 'If our sons were alive they would be like this.' The nine became angry with Salih, because he had been the cause of the killing of their sons. They swore by Allah: 'We will surely raid him and his family by night.' They said: 'We will go out and let people see that we have set out on our journey; then we will come to the cave, remain there until night, and when Salih goes out to his mosque, we will come upon him and kill him; then we will return to the cave and stay there, then return and say: we witnessed the destruction of his family, and we are truthful.' They would be believed, since they would be known to have set out on their journey. Salih (ﷺ) did not sleep with them in the town; he had a mosque called the Mosque of Salih, where he spent the night. When morning came he came to them and admonished and reminded them; when evening came he went out to the mosque and spent the night there. They set out, and when they entered the cave and wanted to come out of the mountain, the cave collapsed upon them and killed them. A man among them who had been informed of that went out and found them crushed, so he returned and began shouting in the town: 'O servants of Allah, has Salih not been satisfied that he commanded them to kill their children, until he killed them?' The people of the town then gathered to hamstring the she-camel."

Ibn Ishaq said: The nine's agreement to kill Salih (ﷺ) was only after they had hamstrung the she-camel and after Salih warned them of punishment. The nine who hamstrung the she-camel said: "Come, let us kill Salih; if he is truthful we will hasten his killing, and if he is lying we will send him to join his camel." They came to him at night to attack him in his household, but the angels repelled them with stones. When they were late returning to their companions, they came to Salih's house and found them crushed, struck with stones. They said to Salih: "You killed them." Then they resolved against him, but his clan stood between them and him and put on their weapons, and said to them: "By Allah, you will never kill him, and he has promised you that punishment will descend upon you in three days. If he is truthful, you will only increase your Lord's anger; and if he is lying, you will be free of what you intend." They turned away from them that night.

Al-Suddi and others said: The worst child, meaning Qudar, grew in a day what others grew in a week, and in a month what others grew in a year. When he grew up, he sat with people who drank wine. They wanted something to mix with their drink, and that day was the she-camel's turn to drink, and they found that the water had been drunk by the she-camel. That was hard for them, and they spoke about the she-camel and her hardship upon them: "We do not do anything with milk; if we took from this water the she-camel drinks, and gave it to our livestock and crops, it would be better for us." The son of the tenth said: "Shall I hamstring her for you?" They said: "Yes."

Ka'b said: The cause of their hamstringing the she-camel was that a woman called Malka had ruled Thamud. When people turned to Salih and leadership passed to him, she envied him; she said to a woman called Qatam, who was the beloved of Qudar ibn Salif, and to another woman called Qabal, who was the beloved of Mus'ad ibn Mahraj (also said ibn Wa'd), and Qudar and Mus'ad used to meet every night with them and drink wine. Malka said to them: "If Qudar and Mus'ad come to you tonight, do not obey them; tell them: 'The queen is sad because of the she-camel and because of Salih; we will not obey you until you hamstring the she-camel; if you hamstring her, we will obey you.'" When they came to them, the two women said this to them, and they said: [...]

Ibn Ishaq and others said: Qudar, Mus'ad and their seven companions set out, lay in wait for the she-camel when she came back from the water, and Qudar lay in wait for her at the base of a pit on her path, and Mus'ad lay in wait on another path. She passed by Mus'ad, who shot her with an arrow that struck the muscle of her leg, and Umm Ghanm and 'Unayza came out and ordered their daughter, who was among the most beautiful people, to show herself to Qudar; then she [Qudar] came to the she-camel and struck her with the sword, cutting her hamstring. She went out roaring one roar, then her young one ran off, and he thrust a spear into her chest and slaughtered her.

The people of the town came out and divided her meat and cooked it. When her young one (that is, her offspring) saw that, he went off until he reached a strong mountain called Sur; it was also said its name was Qara. He came to Salih and said: "Catch up with the she-camel, she has been hamstrung." They came out to meet him, apologizing to him: "O Prophet of Allah, it was only so-and-so and so-and-so who hamstrung her; we are not to blame." Salih (peace be upon him) said: "See whether you can catch up with her young one; if you catch him, perhaps the punishment will be lifted from you." They went out seeking him, and when they saw him on the mountain they went to seize him, but Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed to the mountain, and it rose up into the sky until no bird could reach it. Salih (peace be upon him) came, and when the young one saw him he wept until his tears flowed, then he faced Salih and cried out one cry, then another, then another.

Salih (peace be upon him) said: "For every cry there is a term. Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days; that is a promise not to be denied" [Hud 65].

Ibn Ishaq said: Four men followed the young camel (al-saqb) from among the nine who had hamstrung the she-camel, and among them were Mus'da' ibn Mahraj and his brother Dab ibn Mahraj. Mus'da' shot an arrow that pierced its heart, then dragged it by its leg and brought it down, and they threw its flesh together with the flesh of its mother. Salih said to them: "You have violated the sanctity of God the Exalted, so await the punishment and vengeance of God." They said to him, mocking him: "And when will that be, O Salih, and what is its sign?" They used to name the days: the first day was Ahad, Monday was Ahwan (Umayyin), Tuesday was Dabar, Wednesday was Jubar, Thursday was Mu'nis, Friday was Ghurubah, and Saturday was Shiyar. They had hamstrung the she-camel on Wednesday, so Salih (peace be upon him) said to them when they said that: "You will become (lit. you will awake) on the day of Mu'nis with your faces yellow; then you will awake on the day of Ghurubah with your faces red; then you will awake on the day of Shiyar with your faces black; then the punishment will overtake you on the day of the first (Ahad)." So they awoke on Thursday with their faces yellow, as if they had been smeared with saffron (khaluq), young and old, male and female alike. They became certain of the punishment and knew that Salih had spoken the truth, so they sought him in order to kill him. Salih went out fleeing until he took refuge with a clan of Thamud called Banu Ghanm. A man of theirs called Nufayl, whose kunya was Abu Hadab, and who was a polytheist, hosted him and hid him, so they could not reach him. They then sat with Salih's companions, torturing them so that they would point out his whereabouts.

A man among Salih's companions called Mubda' ibn Harim said: "O Prophet of God, they are torturing us so that we will point them to you; shall we point them out?" He said: "Yes." So Mida' (Mubda') pointed them to him, and they came to Abu Hadab and spoke with him about it. He said: "Yes, Salih is with me, and you have no way to reach him." So they turned away from him and left him alone, and what God the Mighty and Majestic had sent down upon them of His punishment occupied them. Some of them began informing others of what they saw in their faces. When they awoke, they all cried out: "Indeed, one day of the term has passed." When they awoke on the second day, their faces were red as if dyed with blood, so they shrieked, wailed and wept, and they recognised the sign of the punishment. When evening came, they all cried out: "Indeed, two days of the term have passed, and the punishment has come upon you." When the third day came, their faces were black as if smeared with fire, so they all cried out together: "The punishment has come upon you."

When it was the night of Sunday, Salih (peace be upon him) left among them, together with those who had believed with him, for Syria, and they settled in the sands of Palestine. When the people awoke, they wrapped themselves in shrouds and applied camphor/aloes-type perfume (hanut), their hanut being sabr and muqar, and their shrouds were [leather mats (anta')]. Then they threw themselves on the ground, turning their eyes: looking at the sky once and at the earth once, not knowing from where the punishment would come upon them.

When the forenoon grew intense on Sunday, a shriek came to them from the sky, containing the sound of every thunderbolt and the sound of everything in the earth that has a sound, so their hearts were torn apart within their chests, and none of them, small or great, was left alive except that they perished, just as God the Exalted said: ﴿So they became prostrate corpses in their homes﴾. Except for a crippled girl among them called Dhari'a bint Salaq, who was a disbeliever and fiercely hostile to Salih (peace be upon him). God the Mighty and Majestic released her leg after she had witnessed the whole punishment, so she went out faster than anything has ever been seen to move, until she reached Qazah [Qazah: a valley in Muzdalifah], which is Wadi al-Qura, and she informed them of what she had witnessed of the punishment and what had befallen Thamud. Then she asked for water and was given some, and when she drank it she died.

Abu al-Zubayr narrated from Jabir ibn Abdullah, who said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered (the army) at the Hijr during the expedition of Tabuk, he said to his companions: "None of you should enter the town, nor drink from its water, nor enter upon these punished people unless you are weeping and fearful; and if you are not, then do not enter upon them, lest there befall you what befell them."

Then he said: "Now then, do not ask your Messenger for signs. These were the people of Salih, who asked their messenger for a sign, so God the Mighty and Majestic sent them the she-camel. She would come to them from this pass and depart by that pass, and she would drink their water on one day, while on the other day they would have water. When the camel's colt climbed up into the cave behind them, they rebelled against the command of their Lord and hamstrung her, so God destroyed from under the expanse of the sky all of them except one man, who was in the sanctuary of God."

It was said: "Who was he?" He said: "Abu Righal." [190]

When he came out, what had befallen his people befell him [and he was buried here], and a golden branch was buried with him. He showed them the grave of Abu Righal, so the people rushed toward it with their swords, dug around it and extracted that branch. Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) lowered his head and hastened his pace until he passed the valley [[in full in Tafsir al-Tabari: 12/85 and Tarikh al-Tabari: 1/159, with variation.]].

The people of knowledge said: Salih (peace be upon him) died in Mecca at the age of fifty-eight, and he remained among his people for twenty years.

From al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim, who said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) said: "O Ali, do you know who is the most wretched of the first?" I said: "God and His Messenger know best."

He said: "The one who hamstrung the she-camel." 

He said: "Do you know who is the most wretched of the last?" I said: "God and His Messenger know best."

He said: "Your slayer." [191] [[al-Tabaqat al-Kubra: 3/35; Tarikh Baghdad: 1/146; Shawahid al-Tanzil: 2/444, no. 1108.]]

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 7, verse 73–79 (part 1 of 2):

And to Thamud [We sent] their brother Salih. Yahya ibn Wathhab recited: "ilā Thamūdin" with tanwin and without the diptote (ṣarf). The rest recited it without ṣarf. What is meant is: "and to the sons of Thamud," and he is Thamud ibn [Ad] ibn Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh, and he is the brother of [Jadis]. Here he intends the tribe.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala said: Thamud was named so for the scarcity of its water, for al-thamd means little water. Their dwellings were the rock-cut houses (al-Hijr) between the Hijaz and al-Sham, up to Wadi al-Qura. [They were sent to] their brother Salih, and he is Salih ibn [Ubayd] ibn Asaf ibn Masikh ibn Ubayd ibn Khadir ibn Thamud. He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. There has certainly come to you clear evidence from your Lord," meaning a proof and a sign from your Lord confirming my truthfulness. "This is the she-camel of Allah for you," He attributed it to Himself as a mark of distinction and specification, as one says "the House of Allah" [[See Tarikh al-Tabari: 1/158.]].

It was also said: she was attributed to Allah because she came into being by [Divine] creation without the union of a male and female, and she was not from a loin or a womb, and creatures had no effort in her. "A sign" is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: look at this she-camel. "Leave her to graze on Allah's earth, and do not touch her with harm, lest a painful punishment seize you." "And remember when He made you successors after 'Ad, and settled you in the land, taking from its plains palaces, and hewing the mountains into houses," [Al-Hasan recited "wa-tanḥatūna" with a fatḥa on the ḥa', which is a dialect form], and they used to carve out houses in the mountains. "So remember the favours of Allah, and do not commit corruption in the land, causing mischief."

"The chiefs of his people who were arrogant said," meaning the nobles and leaders who exalted themselves above faith in Salih (peace be upon him), "to those who were deemed weak," meaning the followers, "among those who believed: Do you know that Salih is sent from his Lord?" They said: "Indeed, we believe in what he has been sent with." Those who were arrogant said: "Indeed, we are disbelievers in that which you believe" (jāḥidūn, deniers). "Then they hamstrung the she-camel," slaughtered her, "and they rebelled against the command of their Lord, and said: O Salih, bring us what you threaten us with," meaning the punishment, "if you are one of the messengers," i.e., one of the truthful. "So the quake seized them," meaning the cry and the earthquake; its root meaning is movement with sound. Allah said: "The day the quaker quakes" [al-Nazi'at 6]. A poet said:

"When the pilgrimage's time had come, the camels of the people shook" ... 
And al-Akhtal said:
"Do you not see me, the white hair of old age has grown upon my temples; I am old like an eagle, the man shaking, weakened by it" ...
[Tafsir al-Tabari: 8/302.]

"So they became in their home," i.e., in their land and their town; that is why "home" is singular. It was also said he meant the dwellings (diyar), and used the singular as in Allah's words: "Indeed, mankind is in loss" [al-'Asr 2]. The meaning of "jathimin" is prostrate, [humbled, struck down], fallen dead; the root of al-jathim is one who sits on his knees.

Jarir said:
"You knew the place of departure and you knew from it the crouching camels like crows" ...
[Tafsir al-Tabari: 8/303.]

"Then he turned away from them," [Salih turned away from them], and said: "O my people, I certainly conveyed to you the message of my Lord and advised you, but you do not love those who give advice." The story of Salih and Thamud and their hamstringing of the she-camel was the cause of their destruction, according to what Ibn Ishaq, al-Suddi, Wahb, Ka'b and others of the People of the Book have mentioned. They said: when 'Ad were destroyed and their affair came to an end, their lifespans were lengthened and they were made successors in the land; they multiplied and prospered there, until one of them would build a dwelling of clay and it would collapse while the man was still alive. When they saw that, they took the mountains as houses, hewed them, bored them, and cut them out, and they were in ease regarding their livelihoods. Then they transgressed against Allah, committed corruption in the land, and worshipped other than Allah. So Allah sent Salih to them. They were Arabs in that place. Salih was among the most noble of them in lineage and the most excellent in standing.

Allah sent him to them while he was young; he called them to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, until he grew gray and old, and none followed him except a few weak ones. When Salih pressed them with supplication and communication, and greatly warned and frightened them, they asked him to show them a sign that would confirm his words. He said: "What sign do you want?" They said: "We want you to come out with us to this festival of ours," and the name of the festival was that they went out to it with their idols on a known day of the year: "you call on your god and we call on ours; if our call is answered, we will follow you, and if yours is answered, you will follow us."

Salih said to them: "Yes." So they went out with their idols to that festival, and Salih went out with them. They called on their idols and asked them that Salih's supplication not be answered in anything. Then Jundu' ibn 'Amr ibn Harash, who was at that time the chief of Thamud, said: "O Salih, bring forth for us from this rock," a single rock in a corner of al-Hijr called al-Katiba, "a she-camel, pregnant (mukhtarijah), hollow-bellied and free of blemish." The mukhtarijah is one resembling the bukht (Bactrian camel) among camels. "If you do it, we will believe you and we will have faith in you." Salih took their covenant that if he did it, they would truly believe him and have faith in him. They said: "Yes."

Salih prayed two rak'as and called on his Lord, and the rock writhed like a woman in labour bringing forth her child, then the hillock moved and split open, bringing forth a she-camel, ten [months pregnant], hollow-bellied and free of blemish, as they had asked. No one knows what is between her sides except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, while they watched; then she gave birth to a young one like her in size. Jundu' ibn 'Amr and a group of his people believed in him. The nobles of Thamud wanted to believe and accept him, but Dhu'ab ibn 'Amr ibn Labid, al-Habbab, the owner of their idols, and Rabab ibn Sam'ar forbade them; they were among the nobles of Thamud. Jundu' ibn 'Amr had a paternal cousin called Shihab ibn Khalifa ibn Makhlah ibn Labid, who wanted to embrace Islam, but that group forbade him and he obeyed them. A man of the family of Thamud said:

"Shihab was called to the religion of the Prophet, and a clan of the family of 'Amr was ready..."
"He intended to respond, had he responded, the mighty of Thamud all together..."
"They did not prefer their companion Dhu'ab, for Salih would have become a mighty one among us..."
"They turned away after their guidance to wolves, but the deviators of the family of Hijr..." [Tafsir al-Tabari: 8/294.]

When the she-camel came out, Salih (peace be upon him) said: "This is a she-camel; she has a share of water, and you have a share of a known day" [al-Shu'ara' 155]. The she-camel remained with her drink in the land of Thamud, grazing on the trees and drinking water. She used to come to the water on the sabbath (sabt); when it was her day, she would put her head into a well in the rock called the Well of the She-Camel, and she would not raise it until she had drunk everything in it, leaving not a drop of water. Then she would raise her head [and spread her legs], meaning she would straddle the way for them, so they could milk as much milk as they wished, and they drank and stored it until they filled all their vessels. Then she would leave by [other than] the narrow passage through which she had come, being unable to exit where she had entered because of its narrowness, and then she would raise her head.

Abu Musa al-Ash'ari said: I came to the land of Thamud and measured the place where the she-camel went out, and I found it sixty cubits. When the next day came, it was their day; they drank as much water as they wished and stored what they wished for the day of the she-camel. They were in ease and tranquility because of that. [The she-camel] would summer, when the heat was there, in the upper part of the valley, and their sheep, cattle and camels would flee from her and descend into the lower part of the valley in its heat and drought. And the livestock would scatter from her when they saw her; she wintered in the lower part of the valley when winter came, so their livestock fled to the upper part of the valley in the cold and drought. That harmed their livestock, as a trial and test. Their pastures, as they claim, were al-Janab and Hasma; all of them grazed along with the Wadi al-Hijr.

That was hard for them, so they transgressed against the command of their Lord, and that led them to hamstring the she-camel, and they agreed to hamstring her.

There was a woman of Thamud called 'Unayza bint Ghanm ibn Mujallaz, kunya Umm Ghanm, from the Banu 'Ubayd ibn al-Muhl, and she was the wife of Dhu'ab ibn 'Amr; she was an old, aged woman who had beautiful daughters and was rich in camels, cattle and sheep. And another woman called Sadduf bint al-Muhayya ibn Zuhayr ibn al-Muhayya, chief of the Banu 'Ubayd and owner of their idols in the earlier time. The valley was called Wadi al-Muhayya al-Akbar, after the grandfather of al-Muhayya al-Asghar, the father of Sadduf. Sadduf was one of the most beautiful people, wealthy, with camels, sheep and cattle. These two were among the fiercest of people in enmity toward Salih (peace be upon him) and the greatest in disbelief in him, and they loved that the she-camel be hamstrung, despite their disbelief, because she harmed their livestock.

Sadduf was under the guardianship of a maternal cousin of hers called Sintam ibn Harawa ibn Sa'd ibn al-Ghatrif from the Banu Hulayl, who embraced Islam and whose Islam was good. Sadduf had entrusted her property to him, and he spent it on those among Salih's companions who had embraced Islam, until the property dwindled. She discovered that because of Sadduf's Islam, and held him to account for it. He then revealed his religion to her, called her to Allah and to Islam, but she refused him, and took her sons and daughters from him, and hid them among the 'Ubayd of her own clan, and Sintam her husband was from the Banu Hulayl, her maternal cousin. He said to her: "Return my children to me." She said: "Until I contend with you before the Banu Sun'an ibn 'Ubayd or the Banu Jundu' ibn 'Ubayd." Sunaym said to her: "Rather, I will contend with you before the Banu Mirdas ibn 'Ubayd." That was because the Banu Mirdas were Muslims.

She said: "I will not contend with you except before whom you invited me to." The Banu Mirdas said: "By Allah, you will give him his children, unwilling or willing." When she saw that, she gave them to him.

Then Sadduf and 'Unayza plotted together to hamstring the she-camel because of the misfortune that had befallen them. Sadduf called a man of Thamud called [al-Habbab] to hamstring the she-camel and offered herself to him if he did it, but he refused her. She then called a paternal cousin of hers called Mus'ad ibn Mahraj ibn al-Muhayya, and made herself available to him on condition that he hamstring the she-camel; he was among the most handsome of people and the wealthiest, and he agreed to that. 'Unayza bint Ghanm called Qudar ibn Salif ibn Jundu' a man from the people of Qirah.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mentioned him and said: "A mighty, fierce, invincible man among his clan was dispatched for her, like Abu Zam'a." [189] [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 30/269.]] His mother's name was Qadir. He was a short, reddish-blue man; they claim he was born of fornication with a man called Sibyan, and he was not of Salif, who was called the "secret one," but he was born on Salif's bed. She said: "I will give you whichever of my daughters you wish, on condition that you hamstring the she-camel." Qudar was mighty and invincible among his people. So Qudar ibn Salif and Mus'ad ibn Mahraj set out and mobilized deviants of Thamud, and seven men followed them; they were nine men, the leader of whom was Huwayl ibn Mistah, maternal uncle of 'Aziz from the people of Hijr, [and Du'ayb] ibn Ghanm ibn Dhagir, Dhu'ab ibn Mahraj ibn Mus'ad, and five whose names were not mentioned to us. They agreed to hamstring the she-camel.

Al-Suddi and others said: Allah revealed to Salih (peace be upon him) that his people would hamstring his she-camel; he told them that. They said: "We would never do that." Salih said: "A boy will be born among your people who will hamstring her, and your destruction will be at his hands." They said: "No son will be born to us in this month except that we will kill him."

He said: "Nine were born to them in that month. They killed their children; then the tenth was born, and he refused to slaughter his son, for he had no son before that. The son of the tenth was red and blue, and grew quickly. Whenever he passed by the nine and they saw him, they said: 'If our sons were alive they would be like this.' The nine became angry with Salih, because he had been the cause of the killing of their sons. They swore by Allah: 'We will surely raid him and his family by night.' They said: 'We will go out and let people see that we have set out on our journey; then we will come to the cave, remain there until night, and when Salih goes out to his mosque, we will come upon him and kill him; then we will return to the cave and stay there, then return and say: we witnessed the destruction of his family, and we are truthful.' They would be believed, since they would be known to have set out on their journey. Salih (ﷺ) did not sleep with them in the town; he had a mosque called the Mosque of Salih, where he spent the night. When morning came he came to them and admonished and reminded them; when evening came he went out to the mosque and spent the night there. They set out, and when they entered the cave and wanted to come out of the mountain, the cave collapsed upon them and killed them. A man among them who had been informed of that went out and found them crushed, so he returned and began shouting in the town: 'O servants of Allah, has Salih not been satisfied that he commanded them to kill their children, until he killed them?' The people of the town then gathered to hamstring the she-camel."

Ibn Ishaq said: The nine's agreement to kill Salih (ﷺ) was only after they had hamstrung the she-camel and after Salih warned them of punishment. The nine who hamstrung the she-camel said: "Come, let us kill Salih; if he is truthful we will hasten his killing, and if he is lying we will send him to join his camel." They came to him at night to attack him in his household, but the angels repelled them with stones. When they were late returning to their companions, they came to Salih's house and found them crushed, struck with stones. They said to Salih: "You killed them." Then they resolved against him, but his clan stood between them and him and put on their weapons, and said to them: "By Allah, you will never kill him, and he has promised you that punishment will descend upon you in three days. If he is truthful, you will only increase your Lord's anger; and if he is lying, you will be free of what you intend." They turned away from them that night.

Al-Suddi and others said: The worst child, meaning Qudar, grew in a day what others grew in a week, and in a month what others grew in a year. When he grew up, he sat with people who drank wine. They wanted something to mix with their drink, and that day was the she-camel's turn to drink, and they found that the water had been drunk by the she-camel. That was hard for them, and they spoke about the she-camel and her hardship upon them: "We do not do anything with milk; if we took from this water the she-camel drinks, and gave it to our livestock and crops, it would be better for us." The son of the tenth said: "Shall I hamstring her for you?" They said: "Yes."

Ka'b said: The cause of their hamstringing the she-camel was that a woman called Malka had ruled Thamud. When people turned to Salih and leadership passed to him, she envied him; she said to a woman called Qatam, who was the beloved of Qudar ibn Salif, and to another woman called Qabal, who was the beloved of Mus'ad ibn Mahraj (also said ibn Wa'd), and Qudar and Mus'ad used to meet every night with them and drink wine. Malka said to them: "If Qudar and Mus'ad come to you tonight, do not obey them; tell them: 'The queen is sad because of the she-camel and because of Salih; we will not obey you until you hamstring the she-camel; if you hamstring her, we will obey you.'" When they came to them, the two women said this to them, and they said: [...]

Ibn Ishaq and others said: Qudar, Mus'ad and their seven companions set out, lay in wait for the she-camel when she came back from the water, and Qudar lay in wait for her at the base of a pit on her path, and Mus'ad lay in wait on another path. She passed by Mus'ad, who shot her with an arrow that struck the muscle of her leg, and Umm Ghanm and 'Unayza came out and ordered their daughter, who was among the most beautiful people, to show herself to Qudar; then she [Qudar] came to the she-camel and struck her with the sword, cutting her hamstring. She went out roaring one roar, then her young one ran off, and he thrust a spear into her chest and slaughtered her.

The people of the town came out and divided her meat and cooked it. When her young one (that is, her offspring) saw that, he went off until he reached a strong mountain called Sur; it was also said its name was Qara. He came to Salih and said: "Catch up with the she-camel, she has been hamstrung." They came out to meet him, apologizing to him: "O Prophet of Allah, it was only so-and-so and so-and-so who hamstrung her; we are not to blame." Salih (peace be upon him) said: "See whether you can catch up with her young one; if you catch him, perhaps the punishment will be lifted from you." They went out seeking him, and when they saw him on the mountain they went to seize him, but Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed to the mountain, and it rose up into the sky until no bird could reach it. Salih (peace be upon him) came, and when the young one saw him he wept until his tears flowed, then he faced Salih and cried out one cry, then another, then another.

Salih (peace be upon him) said: "For every cry there is a term. Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days; that is a promise not to be denied" [Hud 65].

Ibn Ishaq said: Four men followed the young camel (al-saqb) from among the nine who had hamstrung the she-camel, and among them were Mus'da' ibn Mahraj and his brother Dab ibn Mahraj. Mus'da' shot an arrow that pierced its heart, then dragged it by its leg and brought it down, and they threw its flesh together with the flesh of its mother. Salih said to them: "You have violated the sanctity of God the Exalted, so await the punishment and vengeance of God." They said to him, mocking him: "And when will that be, O Salih, and what is its sign?" They used to name the days: the first day was Ahad, Monday was Ahwan (Umayyin), Tuesday was Dabar, Wednesday was Jubar, Thursday was Mu'nis, Friday was Ghurubah, and Saturday was Shiyar. They had hamstrung the she-camel on Wednesday, so Salih (peace be upon him) said to them when they said that: "You will become (lit. you will awake) on the day of Mu'nis with your faces yellow; then you will awake on the day of Ghurubah with your faces red; then you will awake on the day of Shiyar with your faces black; then the punishment will overtake you on the day of the first (Ahad)." So they awoke on Thursday with their faces yellow, as if they had been smeared with saffron (khaluq), young and old, male and female alike. They became certain of the punishment and knew that Salih had spoken the truth, so they sought him in order to kill him. Salih went out fleeing until he took refuge with a clan of Thamud called Banu Ghanm. A man of theirs called Nufayl, whose kunya was Abu Hadab, and who was a polytheist, hosted him and hid him, so they could not reach him. They then sat with Salih's companions, torturing them so that they would point out his whereabouts.

A man among Salih's companions called Mubda' ibn Harim said: "O Prophet of God, they are torturing us so that we will point them to you; shall we point them out?" He said: "Yes." So Mida' (Mubda') pointed them to him, and they came to Abu Hadab and spoke with him about it. He said: "Yes, Salih is with me, and you have no way to reach him." So they turned away from him and left him alone, and what God the Mighty and Majestic had sent down upon them of His punishment occupied them. Some of them began informing others of what they saw in their faces. When they awoke, they all cried out: "Indeed, one day of the term has passed." When they awoke on the second day, their faces were red as if dyed with blood, so they shrieked, wailed and wept, and they recognised the sign of the punishment. When evening came, they all cried out: "Indeed, two days of the term have passed, and the punishment has come upon you." When the third day came, their faces were black as if smeared with fire, so they all cried out together: "The punishment has come upon you."

When it was the night of Sunday, Salih (peace be upon him) left among them, together with those who had believed with him, for Syria, and they settled in the sands of Palestine. When the people awoke, they wrapped themselves in shrouds and applied camphor/aloes-type perfume (hanut), their hanut being sabr and muqar, and their shrouds were [leather mats (anta')]. Then they threw themselves on the ground, turning their eyes: looking at the sky once and at the earth once, not knowing from where the punishment would come upon them.

When the forenoon grew intense on Sunday, a shriek came to them from the sky, containing the sound of every thunderbolt and the sound of everything in the earth that has a sound, so their hearts were torn apart within their chests, and none of them, small or great, was left alive except that they perished, just as God the Exalted said: ﴿So they became prostrate corpses in their homes﴾. Except for a crippled girl among them called Dhari'a bint Salaq, who was a disbeliever and fiercely hostile to Salih (peace be upon him). God the Mighty and Majestic released her leg after she had witnessed the whole punishment, so she went out faster than anything has ever been seen to move, until she reached Qazah [Qazah: a valley in Muzdalifah], which is Wadi al-Qura, and she informed them of what she had witnessed of the punishment and what had befallen Thamud. Then she asked for water and was given some, and when she drank it she died.

Abu al-Zubayr narrated from Jabir ibn Abdullah, who said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered (the army) at the Hijr during the expedition of Tabuk, he said to his companions: "None of you should enter the town, nor drink from its water, nor enter upon these punished people unless you are weeping and fearful; and if you are not, then do not enter upon them, lest there befall you what befell them."

Then he said: "Now then, do not ask your Messenger for signs. These were the people of Salih, who asked their messenger for a sign, so God the Mighty and Majestic sent them the she-camel. She would come to them from this pass and depart by that pass, and she would drink their water on one day, while on the other day they would have water. When the camel's colt climbed up into the cave behind them, they rebelled against the command of their Lord and hamstrung her, so God destroyed from under the expanse of the sky all of them except one man, who was in the sanctuary of God."

It was said: "Who was he?" He said: "Abu Righal." [190]

When he came out, what had befallen his people befell him [and he was buried here], and a golden branch was buried with him. He showed them the grave of Abu Righal, so the people rushed toward it with their swords, dug around it and extracted that branch. Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) lowered his head and hastened his pace until he passed the valley [[in full in Tafsir al-Tabari: 12/85 and Tarikh al-Tabari: 1/159, with variation.]].

The people of knowledge said: Salih (peace be upon him) died in Mecca at the age of fifty-eight, and he remained among his people for twenty years.

From al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim, who said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) said: "O Ali, do you know who is the most wretched of the first?" I said: "God and His Messenger know best."

He said: "The one who hamstrung the she-camel." 

He said: "Do you know who is the most wretched of the last?" I said: "God and His Messenger know best."

He said: "Your slayer." [191] [[al-Tabaqat al-Kubra: 3/35; Tarikh Baghdad: 1/146; Shawahid al-Tanzil: 2/444, no. 1108.]]

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 7, verse 73–79 (part 1 of 2):

And to Thamud [We sent] their brother Salih. Yahya ibn Wathhab recited: "ilā Thamūdin" with tanwin and without the diptote (ṣarf). The rest recited it without ṣarf. What is meant is: "and to the sons of Thamud," and he is Thamud ibn [Ad] ibn Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh, and he is the brother of [Jadis]. Here he intends the tribe.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala said: Thamud was named so for the scarcity of its water, for al-thamd means little water. Their dwellings were the rock-cut houses (al-Hijr) between the Hijaz and al-Sham, up to Wadi al-Qura. [They were sent to] their brother Salih, and he is Salih ibn [Ubayd] ibn Asaf ibn Masikh ibn Ubayd ibn Khadir ibn Thamud. He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. There has certainly come to you clear evidence from your Lord," meaning a proof and a sign from your Lord confirming my truthfulness. "This is the she-camel of Allah for you," He attributed it to Himself as a mark of distinction and specification, as one says "the House of Allah" [[See Tarikh al-Tabari: 1/158.]].

It was also said: she was attributed to Allah because she came into being by [Divine] creation without the union of a male and female, and she was not from a loin or a womb, and creatures had no effort in her. "A sign" is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: look at this she-camel. "Leave her to graze on Allah's earth, and do not touch her with harm, lest a painful punishment seize you." "And remember when He made you successors after 'Ad, and settled you in the land, taking from its plains palaces, and hewing the mountains into houses," [Al-Hasan recited "wa-tanḥatūna" with a fatḥa on the ḥa', which is a dialect form], and they used to carve out houses in the mountains. "So remember the favours of Allah, and do not commit corruption in the land, causing mischief."

"The chiefs of his people who were arrogant said," meaning the nobles and leaders who exalted themselves above faith in Salih (peace be upon him), "to those who were deemed weak," meaning the followers, "among those who believed: Do you know that Salih is sent from his Lord?" They said: "Indeed, we believe in what he has been sent with." Those who were arrogant said: "Indeed, we are disbelievers in that which you believe" (jāḥidūn, deniers). "Then they hamstrung the she-camel," slaughtered her, "and they rebelled against the command of their Lord, and said: O Salih, bring us what you threaten us with," meaning the punishment, "if you are one of the messengers," i.e., one of the truthful. "So the quake seized them," meaning the cry and the earthquake; its root meaning is movement with sound. Allah said: "The day the quaker quakes" [al-Nazi'at 6]. A poet said:

"When the pilgrimage's time had come, the camels of the people shook" ... 
And al-Akhtal said:
"Do you not see me, the white hair of old age has grown upon my temples; I am old like an eagle, the man shaking, weakened by it" ...
[Tafsir al-Tabari: 8/302.]

"So they became in their home," i.e., in their land and their town; that is why "home" is singular. It was also said he meant the dwellings (diyar), and used the singular as in Allah's words: "Indeed, mankind is in loss" [al-'Asr 2]. The meaning of "jathimin" is prostrate, [humbled, struck down], fallen dead; the root of al-jathim is one who sits on his knees.

Jarir said:
"You knew the place of departure and you knew from it the crouching camels like crows" ...
[Tafsir al-Tabari: 8/303.]

"Then he turned away from them," [Salih turned away from them], and said: "O my people, I certainly conveyed to you the message of my Lord and advised you, but you do not love those who give advice." The story of Salih and Thamud and their hamstringing of the she-camel was the cause of their destruction, according to what Ibn Ishaq, al-Suddi, Wahb, Ka'b and others of the People of the Book have mentioned. They said: when 'Ad were destroyed and their affair came to an end, their lifespans were lengthened and they were made successors in the land; they multiplied and prospered there, until one of them would build a dwelling of clay and it would collapse while the man was still alive. When they saw that, they took the mountains as houses, hewed them, bored them, and cut them out, and they were in ease regarding their livelihoods. Then they transgressed against Allah, committed corruption in the land, and worshipped other than Allah. So Allah sent Salih to them. They were Arabs in that place. Salih was among the most noble of them in lineage and the most excellent in standing.

Allah sent him to them while he was young; he called them to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, until he grew gray and old, and none followed him except a few weak ones. When Salih pressed them with supplication and communication, and greatly warned and frightened them, they asked him to show them a sign that would confirm his words. He said: "What sign do you want?" They said: "We want you to come out with us to this festival of ours," and the name of the festival was that they went out to it with their idols on a known day of the year: "you call on your god and we call on ours; if our call is answered, we will follow you, and if yours is answered, you will follow us."

Salih said to them: "Yes." So they went out with their idols to that festival, and Salih went out with them. They called on their idols and asked them that Salih's supplication not be answered in anything. Then Jundu' ibn 'Amr ibn Harash, who was at that time the chief of Thamud, said: "O Salih, bring forth for us from this rock," a single rock in a corner of al-Hijr called al-Katiba, "a she-camel, pregnant (mukhtarijah), hollow-bellied and free of blemish." The mukhtarijah is one resembling the bukht (Bactrian camel) among camels. "If you do it, we will believe you and we will have faith in you." Salih took their covenant that if he did it, they would truly believe him and have faith in him. They said: "Yes."

Salih prayed two rak'as and called on his Lord, and the rock writhed like a woman in labour bringing forth her child, then the hillock moved and split open, bringing forth a she-camel, ten [months pregnant], hollow-bellied and free of blemish, as they had asked. No one knows what is between her sides except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, while they watched; then she gave birth to a young one like her in size. Jundu' ibn 'Amr and a group of his people believed in him. The nobles of Thamud wanted to believe and accept him, but Dhu'ab ibn 'Amr ibn Labid, al-Habbab, the owner of their idols, and Rabab ibn Sam'ar forbade them; they were among the nobles of Thamud. Jundu' ibn 'Amr had a paternal cousin called Shihab ibn Khalifa ibn Makhlah ibn Labid, who wanted to embrace Islam, but that group forbade him and he obeyed them. A man of the family of Thamud said:

"Shihab was called to the religion of the Prophet, and a clan of the family of 'Amr was ready..."
"He intended to respond, had he responded, the mighty of Thamud all together..."
"They did not prefer their companion Dhu'ab, for Salih would have become a mighty one among us..."
"They turned away after their guidance to wolves, but the deviators of the family of Hijr..." [Tafsir al-Tabari: 8/294.]

When the she-camel came out, Salih (peace be upon him) said: "This is a she-camel; she has a share of water, and you have a share of a known day" [al-Shu'ara' 155]. The she-camel remained with her drink in the land of Thamud, grazing on the trees and drinking water. She used to come to the water on the sabbath (sabt); when it was her day, she would put her head into a well in the rock called the Well of the She-Camel, and she would not raise it until she had drunk everything in it, leaving not a drop of water. Then she would raise her head [and spread her legs], meaning she would straddle the way for them, so they could milk as much milk as they wished, and they drank and stored it until they filled all their vessels. Then she would leave by [other than] the narrow passage through which she had come, being unable to exit where she had entered because of its narrowness, and then she would raise her head.

Abu Musa al-Ash'ari said: I came to the land of Thamud and measured the place where the she-camel went out, and I found it sixty cubits. When the next day came, it was their day; they drank as much water as they wished and stored what they wished for the day of the she-camel. They were in ease and tranquility because of that. [The she-camel] would summer, when the heat was there, in the upper part of the valley, and their sheep, cattle and camels would flee from her and descend into the lower part of the valley in its heat and drought. And the livestock would scatter from her when they saw her; she wintered in the lower part of the valley when winter came, so their livestock fled to the upper part of the valley in the cold and drought. That harmed their livestock, as a trial and test. Their pastures, as they claim, were al-Janab and Hasma; all of them grazed along with the Wadi al-Hijr.

That was hard for them, so they transgressed against the command of their Lord, and that led them to hamstring the she-camel, and they agreed to hamstring her.

There was a woman of Thamud called 'Unayza bint Ghanm ibn Mujallaz, kunya Umm Ghanm, from the Banu 'Ubayd ibn al-Muhl, and she was the wife of Dhu'ab ibn 'Amr; she was an old, aged woman who had beautiful daughters and was rich in camels, cattle and sheep. And another woman called Sadduf bint al-Muhayya ibn Zuhayr ibn al-Muhayya, chief of the Banu 'Ubayd and owner of their idols in the earlier time. The valley was called Wadi al-Muhayya al-Akbar, after the grandfather of al-Muhayya al-Asghar, the father of Sadduf. Sadduf was one of the most beautiful people, wealthy, with camels, sheep and cattle. These two were among the fiercest of people in enmity toward Salih (peace be upon him) and the greatest in disbelief in him, and they loved that the she-camel be hamstrung, despite their disbelief, because she harmed their livestock.

Sadduf was under the guardianship of a maternal cousin of hers called Sintam ibn Harawa ibn Sa'd ibn al-Ghatrif from the Banu Hulayl, who embraced Islam and whose Islam was good. Sadduf had entrusted her property to him, and he spent it on those among Salih's companions who had embraced Islam, until the property dwindled. She discovered that because of Sadduf's Islam, and held him to account for it. He then revealed his religion to her, called her to Allah and to Islam, but she refused him, and took her sons and daughters from him, and hid them among the 'Ubayd of her own clan, and Sintam her husband was from the Banu Hulayl, her maternal cousin. He said to her: "Return my children to me." She said: "Until I contend with you before the Banu Sun'an ibn 'Ubayd or the Banu Jundu' ibn 'Ubayd." Sunaym said to her: "Rather, I will contend with you before the Banu Mirdas ibn 'Ubayd." That was because the Banu Mirdas were Muslims.

She said: "I will not contend with you except before whom you invited me to." The Banu Mirdas said: "By Allah, you will give him his children, unwilling or willing." When she saw that, she gave them to him.

Then Sadduf and 'Unayza plotted together to hamstring the she-camel because of the misfortune that had befallen them. Sadduf called a man of Thamud called [al-Habbab] to hamstring the she-camel and offered herself to him if he did it, but he refused her. She then called a paternal cousin of hers called Mus'ad ibn Mahraj ibn al-Muhayya, and made herself available to him on condition that he hamstring the she-camel; he was among the most handsome of people and the wealthiest, and he agreed to that. 'Unayza bint Ghanm called Qudar ibn Salif ibn Jundu' a man from the people of Qirah.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mentioned him and said: "A mighty, fierce, invincible man among his clan was dispatched for her, like Abu Zam'a." [189] [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 30/269.]] His mother's name was Qadir. He was a short, reddish-blue man; they claim he was born of fornication with a man called Sibyan, and he was not of Salif, who was called the "secret one," but he was born on Salif's bed. She said: "I will give you whichever of my daughters you wish, on condition that you hamstring the she-camel." Qudar was mighty and invincible among his people. So Qudar ibn Salif and Mus'ad ibn Mahraj set out and mobilized deviants of Thamud, and seven men followed them; they were nine men, the leader of whom was Huwayl ibn Mistah, maternal uncle of 'Aziz from the people of Hijr, [and Du'ayb] ibn Ghanm ibn Dhagir, Dhu'ab ibn Mahraj ibn Mus'ad, and five whose names were not mentioned to us. They agreed to hamstring the she-camel.

Al-Suddi and others said: Allah revealed to Salih (peace be upon him) that his people would hamstring his she-camel; he told them that. They said: "We would never do that." Salih said: "A boy will be born among your people who will hamstring her, and your destruction will be at his hands." They said: "No son will be born to us in this month except that we will kill him."

He said: "Nine were born to them in that month. They killed their children; then the tenth was born, and he refused to slaughter his son, for he had no son before that. The son of the tenth was red and blue, and grew quickly. Whenever he passed by the nine and they saw him, they said: 'If our sons were alive they would be like this.' The nine became angry with Salih, because he had been the cause of the killing of their sons. They swore by Allah: 'We will surely raid him and his family by night.' They said: 'We will go out and let people see that we have set out on our journey; then we will come to the cave, remain there until night, and when Salih goes out to his mosque, we will come upon him and kill him; then we will return to the cave and stay there, then return and say: we witnessed the destruction of his family, and we are truthful.' They would be believed, since they would be known to have set out on their journey. Salih (ﷺ) did not sleep with them in the town; he had a mosque called the Mosque of Salih, where he spent the night. When morning came he came to them and admonished and reminded them; when evening came he went out to the mosque and spent the night there. They set out, and when they entered the cave and wanted to come out of the mountain, the cave collapsed upon them and killed them. A man among them who had been informed of that went out and found them crushed, so he returned and began shouting in the town: 'O servants of Allah, has Salih not been satisfied that he commanded them to kill their children, until he killed them?' The people of the town then gathered to hamstring the she-camel."

Ibn Ishaq said: The nine's agreement to kill Salih (ﷺ) was only after they had hamstrung the she-camel and after Salih warned them of punishment. The nine who hamstrung the she-camel said: "Come, let us kill Salih; if he is truthful we will hasten his killing, and if he is lying we will send him to join his camel." They came to him at night to attack him in his household, but the angels repelled them with stones. When they were late returning to their companions, they came to Salih's house and found them crushed, struck with stones. They said to Salih: "You killed them." Then they resolved against him, but his clan stood between them and him and put on their weapons, and said to them: "By Allah, you will never kill him, and he has promised you that punishment will descend upon you in three days. If he is truthful, you will only increase your Lord's anger; and if he is lying, you will be free of what you intend." They turned away from them that night.

Al-Suddi and others said: The worst child, meaning Qudar, grew in a day what others grew in a week, and in a month what others grew in a year. When he grew up, he sat with people who drank wine. They wanted something to mix with their drink, and that day was the she-camel's turn to drink, and they found that the water had been drunk by the she-camel. That was hard for them, and they spoke about the she-camel and her hardship upon them: "We do not do anything with milk; if we took from this water the she-camel drinks, and gave it to our livestock and crops, it would be better for us." The son of the tenth said: "Shall I hamstring her for you?" They said: "Yes."

Ka'b said: The cause of their hamstringing the she-camel was that a woman called Malka had ruled Thamud. When people turned to Salih and leadership passed to him, she envied him; she said to a woman called Qatam, who was the beloved of Qudar ibn Salif, and to another woman called Qabal, who was the beloved of Mus'ad ibn Mahraj (also said ibn Wa'd), and Qudar and Mus'ad used to meet every night with them and drink wine. Malka said to them: "If Qudar and Mus'ad come to you tonight, do not obey them; tell them: 'The queen is sad because of the she-camel and because of Salih; we will not obey you until you hamstring the she-camel; if you hamstring her, we will obey you.'" When they came to them, the two women said this to them, and they said: [...]

Ibn Ishaq and others said: Qudar, Mus'ad and their seven companions set out, lay in wait for the she-camel when she came back from the water, and Qudar lay in wait for her at the base of a pit on her path, and Mus'ad lay in wait on another path. She passed by Mus'ad, who shot her with an arrow that struck the muscle of her leg, and Umm Ghanm and 'Unayza came out and ordered their daughter, who was among the most beautiful people, to show herself to Qudar; then she [Qudar] came to the she-camel and struck her with the sword, cutting her hamstring. She went out roaring one roar, then her young one ran off, and he thrust a spear into her chest and slaughtered her.

The people of the town came out and divided her meat and cooked it. When her young one (that is, her offspring) saw that, he went off until he reached a strong mountain called Sur; it was also said its name was Qara. He came to Salih and said: "Catch up with the she-camel, she has been hamstrung." They came out to meet him, apologizing to him: "O Prophet of Allah, it was only so-and-so and so-and-so who hamstrung her; we are not to blame." Salih (peace be upon him) said: "See whether you can catch up with her young one; if you catch him, perhaps the punishment will be lifted from you." They went out seeking him, and when they saw him on the mountain they went to seize him, but Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed to the mountain, and it rose up into the sky until no bird could reach it. Salih (peace be upon him) came, and when the young one saw him he wept until his tears flowed, then he faced Salih and cried out one cry, then another, then another.

Salih (peace be upon him) said: "For every cry there is a term. Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days; that is a promise not to be denied" [Hud 65].

Ibn Ishaq said: Four men followed the young camel (al-saqb) from among the nine who had hamstrung the she-camel, and among them were Mus'da' ibn Mahraj and his brother Dab ibn Mahraj. Mus'da' shot an arrow that pierced its heart, then dragged it by its leg and brought it down, and they threw its flesh together with the flesh of its mother. Salih said to them: "You have violated the sanctity of God the Exalted, so await the punishment and vengeance of God." They said to him, mocking him: "And when will that be, O Salih, and what is its sign?" They used to name the days: the first day was Ahad, Monday was Ahwan (Umayyin), Tuesday was Dabar, Wednesday was Jubar, Thursday was Mu'nis, Friday was Ghurubah, and Saturday was Shiyar. They had hamstrung the she-camel on Wednesday, so Salih (peace be upon him) said to them when they said that: "You will become (lit. you will awake) on the day of Mu'nis with your faces yellow; then you will awake on the day of Ghurubah with your faces red; then you will awake on the day of Shiyar with your faces black; then the punishment will overtake you on the day of the first (Ahad)." So they awoke on Thursday with their faces yellow, as if they had been smeared with saffron (khaluq), young and old, male and female alike. They became certain of the punishment and knew that Salih had spoken the truth, so they sought him in order to kill him. Salih went out fleeing until he took refuge with a clan of Thamud called Banu Ghanm. A man of theirs called Nufayl, whose kunya was Abu Hadab, and who was a polytheist, hosted him and hid him, so they could not reach him. They then sat with Salih's companions, torturing them so that they would point out his whereabouts.

A man among Salih's companions called Mubda' ibn Harim said: "O Prophet of God, they are torturing us so that we will point them to you; shall we point them out?" He said: "Yes." So Mida' (Mubda') pointed them to him, and they came to Abu Hadab and spoke with him about it. He said: "Yes, Salih is with me, and you have no way to reach him." So they turned away from him and left him alone, and what God the Mighty and Majestic had sent down upon them of His punishment occupied them. Some of them began informing others of what they saw in their faces. When they awoke, they all cried out: "Indeed, one day of the term has passed." When they awoke on the second day, their faces were red as if dyed with blood, so they shrieked, wailed and wept, and they recognised the sign of the punishment. When evening came, they all cried out: "Indeed, two days of the term have passed, and the punishment has come upon you." When the third day came, their faces were black as if smeared with fire, so they all cried out together: "The punishment has come upon you."

When it was the night of Sunday, Salih (peace be upon him) left among them, together with those who had believed with him, for Syria, and they settled in the sands of Palestine. When the people awoke, they wrapped themselves in shrouds and applied camphor/aloes-type perfume (hanut), their hanut being sabr and muqar, and their shrouds were [leather mats (anta')]. Then they threw themselves on the ground, turning their eyes: looking at the sky once and at the earth once, not knowing from where the punishment would come upon them.

When the forenoon grew intense on Sunday, a shriek came to them from the sky, containing the sound of every thunderbolt and the sound of everything in the earth that has a sound, so their hearts were torn apart within their chests, and none of them, small or great, was left alive except that they perished, just as God the Exalted said: ﴿So they became prostrate corpses in their homes﴾. Except for a crippled girl among them called Dhari'a bint Salaq, who was a disbeliever and fiercely hostile to Salih (peace be upon him). God the Mighty and Majestic released her leg after she had witnessed the whole punishment, so she went out faster than anything has ever been seen to move, until she reached Qazah [Qazah: a valley in Muzdalifah], which is Wadi al-Qura, and she informed them of what she had witnessed of the punishment and what had befallen Thamud. Then she asked for water and was given some, and when she drank it she died.

Abu al-Zubayr narrated from Jabir ibn Abdullah, who said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered (the army) at the Hijr during the expedition of Tabuk, he said to his companions: "None of you should enter the town, nor drink from its water, nor enter upon these punished people unless you are weeping and fearful; and if you are not, then do not enter upon them, lest there befall you what befell them."

Then he said: "Now then, do not ask your Messenger for signs. These were the people of Salih, who asked their messenger for a sign, so God the Mighty and Majestic sent them the she-camel. She would come to them from this pass and depart by that pass, and she would drink their water on one day, while on the other day they would have water. When the camel's colt climbed up into the cave behind them, they rebelled against the command of their Lord and hamstrung her, so God destroyed from under the expanse of the sky all of them except one man, who was in the sanctuary of God."

It was said: "Who was he?" He said: "Abu Righal." [190]

When he came out, what had befallen his people befell him [and he was buried here], and a golden branch was buried with him. He showed them the grave of Abu Righal, so the people rushed toward it with their swords, dug around it and extracted that branch. Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) lowered his head and hastened his pace until he passed the valley [[in full in Tafsir al-Tabari: 12/85 and Tarikh al-Tabari: 1/159, with variation.]].

The people of knowledge said: Salih (peace be upon him) died in Mecca at the age of fifty-eight, and he remained among his people for twenty years.

From al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim, who said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) said: "O Ali, do you know who is the most wretched of the first?" I said: "God and His Messenger know best."

He said: "The one who hamstrung the she-camel." 

He said: "Do you know who is the most wretched of the last?" I said: "God and His Messenger know best."

He said: "Your slayer." [191] [[al-Tabaqat al-Kubra: 3/35; Tarikh Baghdad: 1/146; Shawahid al-Tanzil: 2/444, no. 1108.]]

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 7, verse 73–79 (part 1 of 2):

And to Thamud [We sent] their brother Salih. Yahya ibn Wathhab recited: "ilā Thamūdin" with tanwin and without the diptote (ṣarf). The rest recited it without ṣarf. What is meant is: "and to the sons of Thamud," and he is Thamud ibn [Ad] ibn Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh, and he is the brother of [Jadis]. Here he intends the tribe.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala said: Thamud was named so for the scarcity of its water, for al-thamd means little water. Their dwellings were the rock-cut houses (al-Hijr) between the Hijaz and al-Sham, up to Wadi al-Qura. [They were sent to] their brother Salih, and he is Salih ibn [Ubayd] ibn Asaf ibn Masikh ibn Ubayd ibn Khadir ibn Thamud. He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. There has certainly come to you clear evidence from your Lord," meaning a proof and a sign from your Lord confirming my truthfulness. "This is the she-camel of Allah for you," He attributed it to Himself as a mark of distinction and specification, as one says "the House of Allah" [[See Tarikh al-Tabari: 1/158.]].

It was also said: she was attributed to Allah because she came into being by [Divine] creation without the union of a male and female, and she was not from a loin or a womb, and creatures had no effort in her. "A sign" is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: look at this she-camel. "Leave her to graze on Allah's earth, and do not touch her with harm, lest a painful punishment seize you." "And remember when He made you successors after 'Ad, and settled you in the land, taking from its plains palaces, and hewing the mountains into houses," [Al-Hasan recited "wa-tanḥatūna" with a fatḥa on the ḥa', which is a dialect form], and they used to carve out houses in the mountains. "So remember the favours of Allah, and do not commit corruption in the land, causing mischief."

"The chiefs of his people who were arrogant said," meaning the nobles and leaders who exalted themselves above faith in Salih (peace be upon him), "to those who were deemed weak," meaning the followers, "among those who believed: Do you know that Salih is sent from his Lord?" They said: "Indeed, we believe in what he has been sent with." Those who were arrogant said: "Indeed, we are disbelievers in that which you believe" (jāḥidūn, deniers). "Then they hamstrung the she-camel," slaughtered her, "and they rebelled against the command of their Lord, and said: O Salih, bring us what you threaten us with," meaning the punishment, "if you are one of the messengers," i.e., one of the truthful. "So the quake seized them," meaning the cry and the earthquake; its root meaning is movement with sound. Allah said: "The day the quaker quakes" [al-Nazi'at 6]. A poet said:

"When the pilgrimage's time had come, the camels of the people shook" ... 
And al-Akhtal said:
"Do you not see me, the white hair of old age has grown upon my temples; I am old like an eagle, the man shaking, weakened by it" ...
[Tafsir al-Tabari: 8/302.]

"So they became in their home," i.e., in their land and their town; that is why "home" is singular. It was also said he meant the dwellings (diyar), and used the singular as in Allah's words: "Indeed, mankind is in loss" [al-'Asr 2]. The meaning of "jathimin" is prostrate, [humbled, struck down], fallen dead; the root of al-jathim is one who sits on his knees.

Jarir said:
"You knew the place of departure and you knew from it the crouching camels like crows" ...
[Tafsir al-Tabari: 8/303.]

"Then he turned away from them," [Salih turned away from them], and said: "O my people, I certainly conveyed to you the message of my Lord and advised you, but you do not love those who give advice." The story of Salih and Thamud and their hamstringing of the she-camel was the cause of their destruction, according to what Ibn Ishaq, al-Suddi, Wahb, Ka'b and others of the People of the Book have mentioned. They said: when 'Ad were destroyed and their affair came to an end, their lifespans were lengthened and they were made successors in the land; they multiplied and prospered there, until one of them would build a dwelling of clay and it would collapse while the man was still alive. When they saw that, they took the mountains as houses, hewed them, bored them, and cut them out, and they were in ease regarding their livelihoods. Then they transgressed against Allah, committed corruption in the land, and worshipped other than Allah. So Allah sent Salih to them. They were Arabs in that place. Salih was among the most noble of them in lineage and the most excellent in standing.

Allah sent him to them while he was young; he called them to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, until he grew gray and old, and none followed him except a few weak ones. When Salih pressed them with supplication and communication, and greatly warned and frightened them, they asked him to show them a sign that would confirm his words. He said: "What sign do you want?" They said: "We want you to come out with us to this festival of ours," and the name of the festival was that they went out to it with their idols on a known day of the year: "you call on your god and we call on ours; if our call is answered, we will follow you, and if yours is answered, you will follow us."

Salih said to them: "Yes." So they went out with their idols to that festival, and Salih went out with them. They called on their idols and asked them that Salih's supplication not be answered in anything. Then Jundu' ibn 'Amr ibn Harash, who was at that time the chief of Thamud, said: "O Salih, bring forth for us from this rock," a single rock in a corner of al-Hijr called al-Katiba, "a she-camel, pregnant (mukhtarijah), hollow-bellied and free of blemish." The mukhtarijah is one resembling the bukht (Bactrian camel) among camels. "If you do it, we will believe you and we will have faith in you." Salih took their covenant that if he did it, they would truly believe him and have faith in him. They said: "Yes."

Salih prayed two rak'as and called on his Lord, and the rock writhed like a woman in labour bringing forth her child, then the hillock moved and split open, bringing forth a she-camel, ten [months pregnant], hollow-bellied and free of blemish, as they had asked. No one knows what is between her sides except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, while they watched; then she gave birth to a young one like her in size. Jundu' ibn 'Amr and a group of his people believed in him. The nobles of Thamud wanted to believe and accept him, but Dhu'ab ibn 'Amr ibn Labid, al-Habbab, the owner of their idols, and Rabab ibn Sam'ar forbade them; they were among the nobles of Thamud. Jundu' ibn 'Amr had a paternal cousin called Shihab ibn Khalifa ibn Makhlah ibn Labid, who wanted to embrace Islam, but that group forbade him and he obeyed them. A man of the family of Thamud said:

"Shihab was called to the religion of the Prophet, and a clan of the family of 'Amr was ready..."
"He intended to respond, had he responded, the mighty of Thamud all together..."
"They did not prefer their companion Dhu'ab, for Salih would have become a mighty one among us..."
"They turned away after their guidance to wolves, but the deviators of the family of Hijr..." [Tafsir al-Tabari: 8/294.]

When the she-camel came out, Salih (peace be upon him) said: "This is a she-camel; she has a share of water, and you have a share of a known day" [al-Shu'ara' 155]. The she-camel remained with her drink in the land of Thamud, grazing on the trees and drinking water. She used to come to the water on the sabbath (sabt); when it was her day, she would put her head into a well in the rock called the Well of the She-Camel, and she would not raise it until she had drunk everything in it, leaving not a drop of water. Then she would raise her head [and spread her legs], meaning she would straddle the way for them, so they could milk as much milk as they wished, and they drank and stored it until they filled all their vessels. Then she would leave by [other than] the narrow passage through which she had come, being unable to exit where she had entered because of its narrowness, and then she would raise her head.

Abu Musa al-Ash'ari said: I came to the land of Thamud and measured the place where the she-camel went out, and I found it sixty cubits. When the next day came, it was their day; they drank as much water as they wished and stored what they wished for the day of the she-camel. They were in ease and tranquility because of that. [The she-camel] would summer, when the heat was there, in the upper part of the valley, and their sheep, cattle and camels would flee from her and descend into the lower part of the valley in its heat and drought. And the livestock would scatter from her when they saw her; she wintered in the lower part of the valley when winter came, so their livestock fled to the upper part of the valley in the cold and drought. That harmed their livestock, as a trial and test. Their pastures, as they claim, were al-Janab and Hasma; all of them grazed along with the Wadi al-Hijr.

That was hard for them, so they transgressed against the command of their Lord, and that led them to hamstring the she-camel, and they agreed to hamstring her.

There was a woman of Thamud called 'Unayza bint Ghanm ibn Mujallaz, kunya Umm Ghanm, from the Banu 'Ubayd ibn al-Muhl, and she was the wife of Dhu'ab ibn 'Amr; she was an old, aged woman who had beautiful daughters and was rich in camels, cattle and sheep. And another woman called Sadduf bint al-Muhayya ibn Zuhayr ibn al-Muhayya, chief of the Banu 'Ubayd and owner of their idols in the earlier time. The valley was called Wadi al-Muhayya al-Akbar, after the grandfather of al-Muhayya al-Asghar, the father of Sadduf. Sadduf was one of the most beautiful people, wealthy, with camels, sheep and cattle. These two were among the fiercest of people in enmity toward Salih (peace be upon him) and the greatest in disbelief in him, and they loved that the she-camel be hamstrung, despite their disbelief, because she harmed their livestock.

Sadduf was under the guardianship of a maternal cousin of hers called Sintam ibn Harawa ibn Sa'd ibn al-Ghatrif from the Banu Hulayl, who embraced Islam and whose Islam was good. Sadduf had entrusted her property to him, and he spent it on those among Salih's companions who had embraced Islam, until the property dwindled. She discovered that because of Sadduf's Islam, and held him to account for it. He then revealed his religion to her, called her to Allah and to Islam, but she refused him, and took her sons and daughters from him, and hid them among the 'Ubayd of her own clan, and Sintam her husband was from the Banu Hulayl, her maternal cousin. He said to her: "Return my children to me." She said: "Until I contend with you before the Banu Sun'an ibn 'Ubayd or the Banu Jundu' ibn 'Ubayd." Sunaym said to her: "Rather, I will contend with you before the Banu Mirdas ibn 'Ubayd." That was because the Banu Mirdas were Muslims.

She said: "I will not contend with you except before whom you invited me to." The Banu Mirdas said: "By Allah, you will give him his children, unwilling or willing." When she saw that, she gave them to him.

Then Sadduf and 'Unayza plotted together to hamstring the she-camel because of the misfortune that had befallen them. Sadduf called a man of Thamud called [al-Habbab] to hamstring the she-camel and offered herself to him if he did it, but he refused her. She then called a paternal cousin of hers called Mus'ad ibn Mahraj ibn al-Muhayya, and made herself available to him on condition that he hamstring the she-camel; he was among the most handsome of people and the wealthiest, and he agreed to that. 'Unayza bint Ghanm called Qudar ibn Salif ibn Jundu' a man from the people of Qirah.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mentioned him and said: "A mighty, fierce, invincible man among his clan was dispatched for her, like Abu Zam'a." [189] [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 30/269.]] His mother's name was Qadir. He was a short, reddish-blue man; they claim he was born of fornication with a man called Sibyan, and he was not of Salif, who was called the "secret one," but he was born on Salif's bed. She said: "I will give you whichever of my daughters you wish, on condition that you hamstring the she-camel." Qudar was mighty and invincible among his people. So Qudar ibn Salif and Mus'ad ibn Mahraj set out and mobilized deviants of Thamud, and seven men followed them; they were nine men, the leader of whom was Huwayl ibn Mistah, maternal uncle of 'Aziz from the people of Hijr, [and Du'ayb] ibn Ghanm ibn Dhagir, Dhu'ab ibn Mahraj ibn Mus'ad, and five whose names were not mentioned to us. They agreed to hamstring the she-camel.

Al-Suddi and others said: Allah revealed to Salih (peace be upon him) that his people would hamstring his she-camel; he told them that. They said: "We would never do that." Salih said: "A boy will be born among your people who will hamstring her, and your destruction will be at his hands." They said: "No son will be born to us in this month except that we will kill him."

He said: "Nine were born to them in that month. They killed their children; then the tenth was born, and he refused to slaughter his son, for he had no son before that. The son of the tenth was red and blue, and grew quickly. Whenever he passed by the nine and they saw him, they said: 'If our sons were alive they would be like this.' The nine became angry with Salih, because he had been the cause of the killing of their sons. They swore by Allah: 'We will surely raid him and his family by night.' They said: 'We will go out and let people see that we have set out on our journey; then we will come to the cave, remain there until night, and when Salih goes out to his mosque, we will come upon him and kill him; then we will return to the cave and stay there, then return and say: we witnessed the destruction of his family, and we are truthful.' They would be believed, since they would be known to have set out on their journey. Salih (ﷺ) did not sleep with them in the town; he had a mosque called the Mosque of Salih, where he spent the night. When morning came he came to them and admonished and reminded them; when evening came he went out to the mosque and spent the night there. They set out, and when they entered the cave and wanted to come out of the mountain, the cave collapsed upon them and killed them. A man among them who had been informed of that went out and found them crushed, so he returned and began shouting in the town: 'O servants of Allah, has Salih not been satisfied that he commanded them to kill their children, until he killed them?' The people of the town then gathered to hamstring the she-camel."
