This is supported by the reading of Ibn 'Abbas: "fa-istamarrat bihi" (so she continued with it).

Qatadah said: ﴿fa-marrat bihi﴾ means her pregnancy became evident. Yahya ibn Ya'mar read (fa-marat) with a light "r", from al-mirya (doubt), meaning: she doubted whether she was pregnant or not. ﴿Then when she became heavy﴾ meaning the child grew in her womb and moved, and she became burdened with her pregnancy, as one says "athmara" when he has fruit (thamar). ﴿They both called upon Allah, their Lord﴾ meaning Adam and Eve, ﴿saying: If You give us a righteous one﴾ O our Lord.

Al-Hasan said: a male child. Others said: ﴿a human being, sound like us﴾ ﴿we will surely be among the thankful﴾. This is because they feared that what was in her might be something other than a human, or a deformed being.

Al-Kalbi said: When Eve first became heavy with pregnancy, Iblis came to her in the form of a man and said: "What is this that is in your belly?" She said: "I do not know." He said: "I fear it may be an animal." She told that to Adam, and they remained in comfort from such thoughts. Then he returned to her and said: "I am sent from Allah. If you pray to Allah and she gives birth to a human, will you name him after me?" She said: "Yes." He said: "Then I will pray to Allah." He came to her after she had given birth and said: "Name him after me." She said: "And what is your name?" He said: "al-Harith." Had he named himself, she would have recognised him. So she named him ʿAbd al-Harith.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: When Adam and Eve (peace be upon them) descended to the earth, desire was placed in Adam's soul and he approached her, and she conceived. When her child moved in her womb, Iblis came to her and said: "What is this you see? On earth there is only a she-camel, a cow, a sheep, a goat or the like. How do you know what is in your belly? Perhaps it is a dog, a pig or a donkey. How do you know from where it will come out? From your back passage, killing you, or from your ear or your eyes or your mouth, or it will split your belly and kill you." Eve feared this, and he said: "Then obey me and name him ʿAbd al-Harith. His name among the angels was al-Harith. You will bear one resembling you both." She mentioned that to Adam, and he said: "Perhaps it is our companion whom you know." Iblis kept returning to them until he deceived them, and they named him ʿAbd al-Harith.

Al-Sudi said: Eve bore a boy, and Iblis came to her and said: "Name him after me, or I will kill him." Adam said to him: "I have obeyed you, and you have expelled me from the Garden." He refused to obey him, and the boy died. She conceived another, and when she bore him Iblis said the same, and they refused to obey him, and that child died. She conceived another, and Iblis came to them and said: "If you overcome me, name him ʿAbd al-Harith." The name of Iblis was al-Harith. "They did not perceive him. By Allah, I will not cease to kill them until you name him ʿAbd al-Harith, as I killed the first and the second." So they named him ʿAbd al-Harith, and he lived.

Ibn 'Abbas said: Eve bore children to Adam and named them ʿAbd Allah, ʿUbayd Allah, ʿAbd al-Rahman and the like, and death befell them. Iblis came to them and said: "If you name him ʿAbd al-Harith, a child will live for you." They named him ʿAbd al-Harith, she bore a son, they named him ʿAbd al-Harith, and concerning them Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿Then when He gave them a righteous one﴾ meaning a child, human, sound, living, of the sons of Adam, ﴿they made for Him partners in what He gave them.﴾

Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Aban ibn Tha'lab, 'Asim, 'Ikrimah and the people of Madinah read ﴿shirkan﴾ with a kasra on the shin and tanwin, meaning: a share for Him.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: meaning a portion and share from someone other than Him. The rest read ﴿shurakā'﴾ with a damma on the shin and a long vowel, as the plural of shareek (partner), using the plural for the singular, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿those to whom the people said: Indeed the people have gathered against you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173], where "the people" refers to a single man. The speech ends here; then He said: ﴿Exalted is Allah above what they associate with Him﴾ meaning the people of Makkah.

The scholars differed concerning the interpretation of the "partnership" attributed to Adam and Eve. The exegetes said: it was partnership in naming and attribute, not in worship and lordship.

The people of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: they did not believe that al-Harith was their lord by naming their child ʿAbd al-Harith, but they intended that al-Harith was the cause of the child's safety and his mother's well-being, so they named him after him, just as one names the lord of a house, and just as a man names himself "servant of his guest" out of humility towards him, not because the guest is his lord.

As Hatim said:

And I am the servant of the guest as long as he remains, and there is in me nothing but that trait of the servant.

Some people of knowledge said: this refers to the polytheists among the descendants of Adam, and its meaning is that their children made partners for Him. The children are omitted and the parents put in their place, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82], and as He attributes the deeds of fathers to sons, in the case of the Jews of the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: ﴿Then you took the calf after him﴾, and ﴿and when you killed a soul and disputed about it﴾, and ﴿Why then did you kill the prophets of Allah?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 91] and the like. This is supported by what Ma'mar related from al-Hasan, who said: by this is meant those among the descendants of Adam who associated partners, and it did not mean Adam.

Qatadah related from him that he said: they are the Jews and Christians, whom Allah gave children, and they became Jews and Christians.

Ibn Kaysan said: they are the disbelievers who made for Allah partners: ʿAbd al-ʿUzza and ʿAbd Manat.

ʿIkrimah said: it was not specific to Adam, but it is general to all the children of Adam after Adam.

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: this view is more preferable to the people of reflection, because the first view attaches grave matters to the Prophet of Allah Adam (peace be upon him). This is supported by the plural address in His words: ﴿He is the One who created you from a single soul﴾, then He said: ﴿So when he covered her﴾, turning from that address to a report, meaning: when a man among you covered his wife.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Do they associate with Him what creates nothing, while they themselves are created?﴾ meaning the idols of the disbelievers of Makkah, ﴿while they themselves are created.﴾

Ibn Zayd said: A son was born to Adam and they named him ʿAbd Allah. Iblis came to them and said: "What did you name this son of yours?" Before that, a son had been born to them whom they had named ʿAbd Allah, and he died. They said: "We named him ʿAbd Allah." Iblis said: "Do you think Allah will leave His servant with you? What supports the first view is the reading of al-Sulami: ﴿Do you associate﴾ with the letter "ta" (tushrikun).

﴿And they cannot help them, nor can they help themselves. And if you call them to guidance, they will not follow you. It is alike to you whether you call them or you are silent﴾, meaning the idols, ﴿they will not follow you﴾ because they are not rational. ﴿Indeed those whom you call upon besides Allah are servants like you﴾ created, owned, ordained, subjugated, ﴿like you﴾ similar to you. ﴿So call upon them, and let them respond to you, if you are truthful﴾ that they are gods.

﴿Do they have feet with which they walk? Or do they have hands with which they strike? Or do they have eyes with which they see? Or do they have ears with which they hear?﴾ ﴿Say: Call your partners, O assembly of polytheists, then plot against me, and give me no respite.﴾

He said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "He deceived them twice: he deceived them in the Garden, and he deceived them on the earth." [207] [Tafsir al-Tabari: 9/119.]

What supports the first view is the reading of al-Sulami: ﴿Do you associate﴾ with the letter "ta" (tushrikun).

﴿And they cannot help them, nor can they help themselves. And if you call them to guidance, they will not follow you. It is alike to you whether you call them or you are silent﴾, meaning the idols, ﴿they will not follow you﴾ because they are not rational. ﴿Indeed those whom you call upon besides Allah are servants like you﴾ created, owned, ordained, subjugated, ﴿like you﴾ similar to you. ﴿So call upon them, and let them respond to you, if you are truthful﴾ that they are gods.

﴿Do they have feet with which they walk? Or do they have hands with which they strike? Or do they have eyes with which they see? Or do they have ears with which they hear?﴾ ﴿Say: Call your partners, O assembly of polytheists, then plot against me, and give me no respite.﴾

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 7, verse 189–195:

﴿He is the One who created you from a single soul﴾ meaning Adam (peace be upon him), ﴿and made from it its mate﴾ He created Eve from him, ﴿that he might dwell with her﴾ that he might find comfort in her and take refuge with her to fulfil his need. ﴿So when he covered her﴾ had intercourse with her and had relations with her, ﴿she bore a light burden﴾ which is the man's water, light upon her, ﴿and went about with it﴾ meaning she continued with it, stood and sat, and was not troubled by her burden. This is supported by the reading of Ibn 'Abbas: "fa-istamarrat bihi" (so she continued with it).

Qatadah said: ﴿fa-marrat bihi﴾ means her pregnancy became evident. Yahya ibn Ya'mar read (fa-marat) with a light "r", from al-mirya (doubt), meaning: she doubted whether she was pregnant or not. ﴿Then when she became heavy﴾ meaning the child grew in her womb and moved, and she became burdened with her pregnancy, as one says "athmara" when he has fruit (thamar). ﴿They both called upon Allah, their Lord﴾ meaning Adam and Eve, ﴿saying: If You give us a righteous one﴾ O our Lord.

Al-Hasan said: a male child. Others said: ﴿a human being, sound like us﴾ ﴿we will surely be among the thankful﴾. This is because they feared that what was in her might be something other than a human, or a deformed being.

Al-Kalbi said: When Eve first became heavy with pregnancy, Iblis came to her in the form of a man and said: "What is this that is in your belly?" She said: "I do not know." He said: "I fear it may be an animal." She told that to Adam, and they remained in comfort from such thoughts. Then he returned to her and said: "I am sent from Allah. If you pray to Allah and she gives birth to a human, will you name him after me?" She said: "Yes." He said: "Then I will pray to Allah." He came to her after she had given birth and said: "Name him after me." She said: "And what is your name?" He said: "al-Harith." Had he named himself, she would have recognised him. So she named him ʿAbd al-Harith.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: When Adam and Eve (peace be upon them) descended to the earth, desire was placed in Adam's soul and he approached her, and she conceived. When her child moved in her womb, Iblis came to her and said: "What is this you see? On earth there is only a she-camel, a cow, a sheep, a goat or the like. How do you know what is in your belly? Perhaps it is a dog, a pig or a donkey. How do you know from where it will come out? From your back passage, killing you, or from your ear or your eyes or your mouth, or it will split your belly and kill you." Eve feared this, and he said: "Then obey me and name him ʿAbd al-Harith. His name among the angels was al-Harith. You will bear one resembling you both." She mentioned that to Adam, and he said: "Perhaps it is our companion whom you know." Iblis kept returning to them until he deceived them, and they named him ʿAbd al-Harith.

Al-Sudi said: Eve bore a boy, and Iblis came to her and said: "Name him after me, or I will kill him." Adam said to him: "I have obeyed you, and you have expelled me from the Garden." He refused to obey him, and the boy died. She conceived another, and when she bore him Iblis said the same, and they refused to obey him, and that child died. She conceived another, and Iblis came to them and said: "If you overcome me, name him ʿAbd al-Harith." The name of Iblis was al-Harith. "They did not perceive him. By Allah, I will not cease to kill them until you name him ʿAbd al-Harith, as I killed the first and the second." So they named him ʿAbd al-Harith, and he lived.

Ibn 'Abbas said: Eve bore children to Adam and named them ʿAbd Allah, ʿUbayd Allah, ʿAbd al-Rahman and the like, and death befell them. Iblis came to them and said: "If you name him ʿAbd al-Harith, a child will live for you." They named him ʿAbd al-Harith, she bore a son, they named him ʿAbd al-Harith, and concerning them Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿Then when He gave them a righteous one﴾ meaning a child, human, sound, living, of the sons of Adam, ﴿they made for Him partners in what He gave them.﴾

Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Aban ibn Tha'lab, 'Asim, 'Ikrimah and the people of Madinah read ﴿shirkan﴾ with a kasra on the shin and tanwin, meaning: a share for Him.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: meaning a portion and share from someone other than Him. The rest read ﴿shurakā'﴾ with a damma on the shin and a long vowel, as the plural of shareek (partner), using the plural for the singular, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿those to whom the people said: Indeed the people have gathered against you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173], where "the people" refers to a single man. The speech ends here; then He said: ﴿Exalted is Allah above what they associate with Him﴾ meaning the people of Makkah.

The scholars differed concerning the interpretation of the "partnership" attributed to Adam and Eve. The exegetes said: it was partnership in naming and attribute, not in worship and lordship.

The people of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: they did not believe that al-Harith was their lord by naming their child ʿAbd al-Harith, but they intended that al-Harith was the cause of the child's safety and his mother's well-being, so they named him after him, just as one names the lord of a house, and just as a man names himself "servant of his guest" out of humility towards him, not because the guest is his lord.

As Hatim said:

And I am the servant of the guest as long as he remains, and there is in me nothing but that trait of the servant.

Some people of knowledge said: this refers to the polytheists among the descendants of Adam, and its meaning is that their children made partners for Him. The children are omitted and the parents put in their place, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82], and as He attributes the deeds of fathers to sons, in the case of the Jews of the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: ﴿Then you took the calf after him﴾, and ﴿and when you killed a soul and disputed about it﴾, and ﴿Why then did you kill the prophets of Allah?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 91] and the like. This is supported by what Ma'mar related from al-Hasan, who said: by this is meant those among the descendants of Adam who associated partners, and it did not mean Adam.

Qatadah related from him that he said: they are the Jews and Christians, whom Allah gave children, and they became Jews and Christians.

Ibn Kaysan said: they are the disbelievers who made for Allah partners: ʿAbd al-ʿUzza and ʿAbd Manat.

ʿIkrimah said: it was not specific to Adam, but it is general to all the children of Adam after Adam.

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: this view is more preferable to the people of reflection, because the first view attaches grave matters to the Prophet of Allah Adam (peace be upon him). This is supported by the plural address in His words: ﴿He is the One who created you from a single soul﴾, then He said: ﴿So when he covered her﴾, turning from that address to a report, meaning: when a man among you covered his wife.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Do they associate with Him what creates nothing, while they themselves are created?﴾ meaning the idols of the disbelievers of Makkah, ﴿while they themselves are created.﴾

Ibn Zayd said: A son was born to Adam and they named him ʿAbd Allah. Iblis came to them and said: "What did you name this son of yours?" Before that, a son had been born to them whom they had named ʿAbd Allah, and he died. They said: "We named him ʿAbd Allah." Iblis said: "Do you think Allah will leave His servant with you? No, by Allah, he will surely go as the other went. But I will direct you to a name that will remain for you as long as you live." So they named him ʿAbd Shams.

That is His words: ﴿Do they associate what creates nothing, while they themselves are created?﴾ The sun does not create anything, unless it is a servant of Him; rather it is itself created.

He said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "He deceived them twice: he deceived them in the Garden, and he deceived them on the earth." [207] [Tafsir al-Tabari: 9/119.]

What supports the first view is the reading of al-Sulami: ﴿Do you associate﴾ with the letter "ta" (tushrikun).

﴿And they cannot help them, nor can they help themselves. And if you call them to guidance, they will not follow you. It is alike to you whether you call them or you are silent﴾, meaning the idols, ﴿they will not follow you﴾ because they are not rational. ﴿Indeed those whom you call upon besides Allah are servants like you﴾ created, owned, ordained, subjugated, ﴿like you﴾ similar to you. ﴿So call upon them, and let them respond to you, if you are truthful﴾ that they are gods.

﴿Do they have feet with which they walk? Or do they have hands with which they strike? Or do they have eyes with which they see? Or do they have ears with which they hear?﴾ ﴿Say: Call your partners, O assembly of polytheists, then plot against me, and give me no respite.﴾

﴿Indeed, my Guardian is Allah, who sent down the Book, and He takes charge of the righteous.﴾ "Alladhi" means: the One who will protect me and keep me from you.

﴿As for those you call upon besides Him, they cannot help you, nor can they help themselves.﴾ ﴿And if you call them to guidance, they do not hear. And you see them, O Muhammad, looking at you, but they do not see.﴾ "They" means the idols. This is like what the Arabs say: "My house looks at your house," meaning it faces it.

The Arabs also say: "If you come to such-and-such a place and the mountain looks at you, take right or left," meaning: it faces you.

Abu 'Ubayda narrated from al-Kisa'i, who said: "The wall looks at you when it is near you, where you can see it." From this is the poet's saying:

When the lands of Banu Tamim look,
with an eye or without the eye of Banu Sabah...¹

I heard Abu al-Qasim al-Habibi say: I heard Abu Zakariyya al-'Anbari say: The meaning is: "And you see them" as though they were looking at you, like His saying: ﴿And you see people drunken, though they are not drunken﴾² meaning: as though they were drunk. He reported about them using the masculine pronoun (hum), because they are shaped in the form of the sons of Adam, reporting about them by their actions.

﴿Take what is easy.﴾ Mujahid said: It means forgiveness of the people's characters and deeds, without searching them out.

Ibn al-Zubayr said: Allah did not reveal this verse except concerning the people's characters.

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi said: It means what is given to you freely from their wealth, the surplus of dependents and of everything. "So whatever they bring you freely, take it, and do not ask them about what is beyond that."

This was before the obligatory charity (zakat) was revealed. When the verse of charity was revealed, this verse was abrogated (naskh), and he was commanded to take it from them, willingly or by force.

﴿And enjoin what is good (al-'urf)﴾, meaning: what is known as good (al-ma'ruf). 'Isa ibn 'Umar recited "al-'urf" with two dammas, like "al-hilm," and both are dialectal variants. "Al-'urf" is what is known, and "al-'arifa" is every praiseworthy quality that the intellects approve and that souls find reassuring. The poet said:

Whoever does good will not lack one who repays him;
good deeds do not vanish between Allah and the people.³

'Ata' said: "Enjoin what is good" means: there is no god but Allah. ﴿And turn away from the ignorant﴾, meaning Abu Jahl and his companions. It was abrogated by the verse of the sword.

It is said that when this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Jibril: "What is this?" He said: "I do not know until I ask." Then he returned and said: "O Muhammad, your Lord commands you to join ties with the one who cuts you off, to give to the one who withholds from you, and to pardon the one who wronged you."⁴

The poet composed:

The noble qualities are in three;
whoever has them perfected is a man of virtue:
giving to the one who denies you, joining ties with
the one who cuts you off, and pardoning the one who transgresses against you.

Ja'far al-Sadiq said: "Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) with the noble qualities, and there is no verse in the Qur'an more comprehensive of the noble qualities than this verse."⁵

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: (May Allah have mercy on them both).⁶

'A'isha said: The noble qualities are ten: truthfulness of speech; truthfulness in courage in obedience to Allah; giving to the beggar; repaying a favor; joining ties of kinship; fulfilling trusts; honoring one's companion; honoring one's neighbor; hospitality to the guest; and at their head, modesty.⁷

Abu al-Qasim al-Hasan ibn Muhammad, mentioned above, recited to us: Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Saffar recited to us: Ibn Abi al-Dunya recited to us: Abu Ja'far al-Qurashi recited to me:

All matters will leave you and come to an end,
except praise, which remains for you.
If I were given the choice of every virtue,
I would choose nothing but the noble qualities.⁸

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: When this verse was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "How, O Lord, [with anger?]" Then it was revealed: ﴿And if an evil whisper from Satan should come to you, seek refuge in Allah.﴾ Meaning: it may afflict you, tempt you, deceive you, and present itself to you from Satan, a "nazgh" (an incitement).

Its root meaning is an eagerness toward corruption and evil. It is said: "His vein provoked (nazagha 'irquhu)" when it was agitated and stirred up. There are two forms: nazgh and nagh. It is said: "Beware of the nizaʼ and the nighaz," meaning those who incite discord.

Al-Zajjaj said: Nazgh is the least movement that comes from a human, and from Satan, the least whisper. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: I witnessed 'Uthman and 'Ali, and there was an incitement from Satan between them, so neither of them left anything for his companion. Then they did not part until each of them asked forgiveness for the other.⁹

﴿So seek refuge in Allah﴾, meaning: seek protection in Allah. ﴿Indeed He is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾

﴿Indeed, those who have feared Allah﴾, meaning the believers, ﴿when a touch from Satan afflicts them﴾, meaning: strikes them, ﴿a passing thought (ta'if) from Satan.﴾ Al-Nakha'i, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, al-A'mash, Ibn Yazid, al-Jahdari and Talha recited "tayf." The rest recited "ta'if." Both are dialectal variants, like "al-mayt" and "al-mayyit." Their meaning is the thing that comes around you. Some people distinguished between them. Abu 'Amr said: "Ta'if" is what circles around a thing, and "tayf" is the passing impulse, the whisper, the fleeting thought. Some Meccan scholars said: "Ta'if" is what the Satanic whisper circles around, and "tayf" is the flesh and the touch. It is permissible that "tayf" is a lightened form of "tayyif," like "hayyin" and "layyin." This is supported by the recitation of Sa'id ibn Jubayr with the doubled yā' ("tayyif").

Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿When a passing thought from Satan afflicts them﴾ means: an incitement from Satan.

al-Kalbi said: It means a sin. Mujahid said: It means anger.

﴿They remember﴾: they reflect, consider and recognize. Abu Rawq said: They supplicate humbly. In the recitation of 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr: "When a passing thought from Satan afflicts them, they [seek refuge]" (fa-amalu).

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: It is the man who becomes angry, then remembers Allah and restrains his rage. Layth reported from Mujahid: It is the man who intends a sin, then remembers Allah and leaves it. al-Suddi said: It means: if they slip, they repent. Muqatil said: If the God-fearing person is struck by an incitement from Satan, he remembers and recognizes that it is sinful, so he sees it clearly, and the incitement to disobey Allah is removed from him. ﴿Then they are seeing clearly﴾: they look at the places of their error through reflection and contemplation, [and turn away], so they refrain. The God-fearing person is one who desires [...] (an illegible word) and sees, so he refrains.

Then he mentioned the disbelievers, saying: ﴿But their brothers﴾ (i.e., the brothers of the devils, who are the disbelievers), ﴿the devils extend them in error, and then they do not cease.﴾ The devils extend them in error until they seek them out and increase them in misguidance.

The people of Medina recited "yumiddūnahum" with a damma on the yā' and a kasra on the mīm, and both are dialects with the same meaning. al-Jahdari recited "yumadiʼūnahum" in the form of "yufā'ilūnahum."

﴿Then they do not cease﴾, meaning: they do not doubt and do not incite. Ibn Zayd said: They do not grow weary and do not slacken.

Ibn 'Abbas said: Neither humans cease from the evil deeds they do, nor do the jinn refrain from them.

'Isa ibn 'Umar recited "yaqṣurūn" with a fatha on the yā' and a damma on the ṣād. "Qaṣara" and "aqṣara" are one (in meaning).

﴿And when you do not bring them a sign, O Muhammad,﴾ meaning the polytheists, ﴿they say: "Why do you not invent it?"⁠﴾ meaning: why did you not fabricate it and originate it from yourself and by your own choice? This was said by Qatada. Mujahid said: "Why did you not contrive it and bring it out from yourself?"

Ibn Zayd said: "Why do you not choose it and bring it from yourself?"

Ibn 'Abbas said: "Why did you not receive it from yourself, or why did you not narrate it and originate it?" Al-'Awfi reported from Ibn 'Abbas: "You forgot it and invented it from your Lord."

al-Dahhak said: "Why did you not take it yourself and bring it from heaven?" al-Farra' said: The Arabs say: "I fabricated the speech, composed it, improvised it, and adopted it" when a man makes it up from himself.

Ibn Zayd said: The Arabs say that speech only to pacify a man, and he had not prepared it for himself beforehand.

﴿Say, O Muhammad: "I only follow what is revealed to me from my Lord."⁠﴾ Then He said: ﴿This (the Qur'an) is insights (basa'ir), proofs, clarity and evidence from your Lord.﴾ Its singular is "basīra." Al-Zajjaj said: Paths from your Lord; and "al-basā'ir" are the paths of blood (i.e., veins).

al-Ju'fi said:

They went with their insights on their shoulders,
and my insight runs with it, a sturdy steed...¹⁰

They pass beyond my enmity. Its root meaning is the manifestation and establishment of a thing until a person sees it, is guided by it, and benefits from it. From this is said: "I have no insight (basīra) in the matter."¹¹

﴿And guidance and mercy for a people who believe.﴾

﴿When the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent﴾. 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: We used to greet one another in prayer, saying "Peace be upon so-and-so, peace be upon so-and-so." Then this verse came: ﴿When the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent﴾, meaning during the prayer.

Abu Hurayra said: They used to speak during the prayer, and then this verse came and they were commanded to be silent.

al-Zuhri said: This verse was revealed concerning a young man from the Ansar. Whenever the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited something, he would recite it too. So this verse was revealed.

Dawud ibn Abi Hind narrated from Bashir ibn Jabir, who said: Ibn Mas'ud prayed and heard some people reciting along with the imam. When he finished he said: "Has it not yet come time for you to understand? Has it not yet come time for you to reflect? ﴿When the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent﴾, as Allah has commanded you."¹²

al-Hariri narrated from Talha ibn 'Ubayd Allah ibn Kuraiz, who said: I saw 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr and 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah talking while the reader was reciting. I said: "Will you not listen to the remembrance and attend to what is promised?" He said: They looked at me, then turned back to their conversation. I repeated it a second time, and they looked at me and said: "That is only during the prayer: ﴿When the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent.﴾"

Zayd ibn Aslam narrated from his father, from Abu Hurayra, who said: This verse was revealed concerning raising voices while they were behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the prayer.¹³

al-Kalbi said: They used to raise their voices in prayer until they heard mention of Paradise and Hell, so Allah the Exalted revealed this verse.

Qatada said: At the beginning when it was prescribed for them, they used to speak in the prayer about their needs. A man would come while they were praying and ask them: "How many have you prayed? How many remain?" So Allah the Mighty and Majestic revealed this verse.¹⁴

Ibn 'Abbas said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited in the silent prayer, and his companions recited behind him raising their voices, so they confused him, and this verse was revealed.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: The polytheists would come to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he prayed, and some of them would say to others in Mecca: ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it.⁠﴾ So Allah revealed a reply to them: ﴿When the Qur'an is recited...﴾

Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, 'Ata', 'Amr ibn Dinar, Zayd ibn Aslam, al-Qasim ibn Yasar and Shahr ibn Hawshab said: This is about the sermon: a command to be silent for the imam on Friday.

'Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak said: The evidence for the ruling of this verse concerning the Friday sermon is that you never see a preacher on the pulpit on Friday delivering a sermon who wants to recite a verse from the Qur'an without reciting this verse before the recitation of the Qur'an.

al-Hasan said: This is about the obligatory prayer and during remembrance (dhikr). Mujahid and 'Ata' said: Silence became obligatory in two situations: when a man recites the Qur'an while praying, and when the imam is delivering the sermon.

'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said: Silence is for every preacher's speech, and silence means attentive listening and observance.

The poet said:

"The imam said: 'Obey your leader's command,'
so we did not oppose, and we were silent as they said."¹⁵

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: This is about silence on the two festivals and on Friday, and in what the imam recites aloud.¹⁶

al-Zajjaj said: It is permissible that the meaning of His saying "listen" and "be silent" is: act by what it contains and do not transgress it, because the meaning of someone saying "Allah has heard" is: Allah has answered your supplication.

﴿And remember your Lord within yourself﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: By remembrance he means recitation during the prayer. ﴿Humbly (tadarru')﴾, aloud, ﴿and in fear (khifatan)﴾, ﴿and below the level of loudness﴾, below raising the voice, in a low tone and silence, so that those behind you may hear.

The people of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: ﴿And remember your Lord﴾: be admonished by the Qur'an and believe in its signs. ﴿And remember your Lord﴾ by obedience in what He commands you. ﴿(Tadarru')﴾: humility and submission. ﴿(Khifah)﴾: fear of His punishment. So when you recite, you supplicate to Allah, i.e., ﴿below the level of loudness﴾: a concealment, not a shout.¹⁷

Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj said: He was commanded to remember Him in the heart. And he is commanded to humble himself in supplication and submission.

Raising the voice in supplication is disliked [and the excessive shouting] in supplication.

As for His saying ﴿in the mornings and the evenings (al-ghuduwwi wa al-asal)⁠﴾, it means at dawn and in the evenings. The singular of "al-asal" is "asil," like "ayman" and "yamin." The people of language said: it is the period between the afternoon prayer and sunset.

﴿And do not be among the heedless.⁠﴾

﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord﴾ means the angels. The meaning is nearness through grace and mercy, not nearness in place or in reward.

al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: Allah may be worshipped by others than the angels in meaning. [Those from your Lord] received success and protection.

﴿They do not disdain﴾, meaning they do not act arrogantly or consider themselves great, ﴿from His worship﴾, ﴿and they glorify Him﴾, purify Him, remember Him and say "Glory be to Allah," ﴿and to Him they prostrate﴾, meaning they pray.

Mughira narrated from Ibrahim: If he wishes, he bows; if he wishes, he prostrates.¹⁸

﴿Indeed, my Guardian is Allah, who sent down the Book, and He takes charge of the righteous.﴾ "Alladhi" means: the One who will protect me and keep me from you.

﴿As for those you call upon besides Him, they cannot help you, nor can they help themselves.﴾ ﴿And if you call them to guidance, they do not hear. And you see them, O Muhammad, looking at you, but they do not see.﴾ "They" means the idols. This is like what the Arabs say: "My house looks at your house," meaning it faces it.

The Arabs also say: "If you come to such-and-such a place and the mountain looks at you, take right or left," meaning: it faces you.

Abu 'Ubayda narrated from al-Kisa'i, who said: "The wall looks at you when it is near you, where you can see it." From this is the poet's saying:

When the lands of Banu Tamim look,
with an eye or without the eye of Banu Sabah...¹

I heard Abu al-Qasim al-Habibi say: I heard Abu Zakariyya al-'Anbari say: The meaning is: "And you see them" as though they were looking at you, like His saying: ﴿And you see people drunken, though they are not drunken﴾² meaning: as though they were drunk. He reported about them using the masculine pronoun (hum), because they are shaped in the form of the sons of Adam, reporting about them by their actions.

﴿Take what is easy.﴾ Mujahid said: It means forgiveness of the people's characters and deeds, without searching them out.

Ibn al-Zubayr said: Allah did not reveal this verse except concerning the people's characters.

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi said: It means what is given to you freely from their wealth, the surplus of dependents and of everything. "So whatever they bring you freely, take it, and do not ask them about what is beyond that."

This was before the obligatory charity (zakat) was revealed. When the verse of charity was revealed, this verse was abrogated (naskh), and he was commanded to take it from them, willingly or by force.

﴿And enjoin what is good (al-'urf)﴾, meaning: what is known as good (al-ma'ruf). 'Isa ibn 'Umar recited "al-'urf" with two dammas, like "al-hilm," and both are dialectal variants. "Al-'urf" is what is known, and "al-'arifa" is every praiseworthy quality that the intellects approve and that souls find reassuring. The poet said:

Whoever does good will not lack one who repays him;
good deeds do not vanish between Allah and the people.³

'Ata' said: "Enjoin what is good" means: there is no god but Allah. ﴿And turn away from the ignorant﴾, meaning Abu Jahl and his companions. It was abrogated by the verse of the sword.

It is said that when this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Jibril: "What is this?" He said: "I do not know until I ask." Then he returned and said: "O Muhammad, your Lord commands you to join ties with the one who cuts you off, to give to the one who withholds from you, and to pardon the one who wronged you."⁴

The poet composed:

The noble qualities are in three;
whoever has them perfected is a man of virtue:
giving to the one who denies you, joining ties with
the one who cuts you off, and pardoning the one who transgresses against you.

Ja'far al-Sadiq said: "Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) with the noble qualities, and there is no verse in the Qur'an more comprehensive of the noble qualities than this verse."⁵

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: (May Allah have mercy on them both).⁶

'A'isha said: The noble qualities are ten: truthfulness of speech; truthfulness in courage in obedience to Allah; giving to the beggar; repaying a favor; joining ties of kinship; fulfilling trusts; honoring one's companion; honoring one's neighbor; hospitality to the guest; and at their head, modesty.⁷

Abu al-Qasim al-Hasan ibn Muhammad, mentioned above, recited to us: Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Saffar recited to us: Ibn Abi al-Dunya recited to us: Abu Ja'far al-Qurashi recited to me:

All matters will leave you and come to an end,
except praise, which remains for you.
If I were given the choice of every virtue,
I would choose nothing but the noble qualities.⁸

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: When this verse was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "How, O Lord, [with anger?]" Then it was revealed: ﴿And if an evil whisper from Satan should come to you, seek refuge in Allah.﴾ Meaning: it may afflict you, tempt you, deceive you, and present itself to you from Satan, a "nazgh" (an incitement).

Its root meaning is an eagerness toward corruption and evil. It is said: "His vein provoked (nazagha 'irquhu)" when it was agitated and stirred up. There are two forms: nazgh and nagh. It is said: "Beware of the nizaʼ and the nighaz," meaning those who incite discord.

Al-Zajjaj said: Nazgh is the least movement that comes from a human, and from Satan, the least whisper. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: I witnessed 'Uthman and 'Ali, and there was an incitement from Satan between them, so neither of them left anything for his companion. Then they did not part until each of them asked forgiveness for the other.⁹

﴿So seek refuge in Allah﴾, meaning: seek protection in Allah. ﴿Indeed He is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾

﴿Indeed, those who have feared Allah﴾, meaning the believers, ﴿when a touch from Satan afflicts them﴾, meaning: strikes them, ﴿a passing thought (ta'if) from Satan.﴾ Al-Nakha'i, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, al-A'mash, Ibn Yazid, al-Jahdari and Talha recited "tayf." The rest recited "ta'if." Both are dialectal variants, like "al-mayt" and "al-mayyit." Their meaning is the thing that comes around you. Some people distinguished between them. Abu 'Amr said: "Ta'if" is what circles around a thing, and "tayf" is the passing impulse, the whisper, the fleeting thought. Some Meccan scholars said: "Ta'if" is what the Satanic whisper circles around, and "tayf" is the flesh and the touch. It is permissible that "tayf" is a lightened form of "tayyif," like "hayyin" and "layyin." This is supported by the recitation of Sa'id ibn Jubayr with the doubled yā' ("tayyif").

Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿When a passing thought from Satan afflicts them﴾ means: an incitement from Satan.

al-Kalbi said: It means a sin. Mujahid said: It means anger.

﴿They remember﴾: they reflect, consider and recognize. Abu Rawq said: They supplicate humbly. In the recitation of 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr: "When a passing thought from Satan afflicts them, they [seek refuge]" (fa-amalu).

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: It is the man who becomes angry, then remembers Allah and restrains his rage. Layth reported from Mujahid: It is the man who intends a sin, then remembers Allah and leaves it. al-Suddi said: It means: if they slip, they repent. Muqatil said: If the God-fearing person is struck by an incitement from Satan, he remembers and recognizes that it is sinful, so he sees it clearly, and the incitement to disobey Allah is removed from him. ﴿Then they are seeing clearly﴾: they look at the places of their error through reflection and contemplation, [and turn away], so they refrain. The God-fearing person is one who desires [...] (an illegible word) and sees, so he refrains.

Then he mentioned the disbelievers, saying: ﴿But their brothers﴾ (i.e., the brothers of the devils, who are the disbelievers), ﴿the devils extend them in error, and then they do not cease.﴾ The devils extend them in error until they seek them out and increase them in misguidance.

The people of Medina recited "yumiddūnahum" with a damma on the yā' and a kasra on the mīm, and both are dialects with the same meaning. al-Jahdari recited "yumadiʼūnahum" in the form of "yufā'ilūnahum."

﴿Then they do not cease﴾, meaning: they do not doubt and do not incite. Ibn Zayd said: They do not grow weary and do not slacken.

Ibn 'Abbas said: Neither humans cease from the evil deeds they do, nor do the jinn refrain from them.

'Isa ibn 'Umar recited "yaqṣurūn" with a fatha on the yā' and a damma on the ṣād. "Qaṣara" and "aqṣara" are one (in meaning).

﴿And when you do not bring them a sign, O Muhammad,﴾ meaning the polytheists, ﴿they say: "Why do you not invent it?"⁠﴾ meaning: why did you not fabricate it and originate it from yourself and by your own choice? This was said by Qatada. Mujahid said: "Why did you not contrive it and bring it out from yourself?"

Ibn Zayd said: "Why do you not choose it and bring it from yourself?"

Ibn 'Abbas said: "Why did you not receive it from yourself, or why did you not narrate it and originate it?" Al-'Awfi reported from Ibn 'Abbas: "You forgot it and invented it from your Lord."

al-Dahhak said: "Why did you not take it yourself and bring it from heaven?" al-Farra' said: The Arabs say: "I fabricated the speech, composed it, improvised it, and adopted it" when a man makes it up from himself.

Ibn Zayd said: The Arabs say that speech only to pacify a man, and he had not prepared it for himself beforehand.

﴿Say, O Muhammad: "I only follow what is revealed to me from my Lord."⁠﴾ Then He said: ﴿This (the Qur'an) is insights (basa'ir), proofs, clarity and evidence from your Lord.﴾ Its singular is "basīra." Al-Zajjaj said: Paths from your Lord; and "al-basā'ir" are the paths of blood (i.e., veins).

al-Ju'fi said:

They went with their insights on their shoulders,
and my insight runs with it, a sturdy steed...¹⁰

They pass beyond my enmity. Its root meaning is the manifestation and establishment of a thing until a person sees it, is guided by it, and benefits from it. From this is said: "I have no insight (basīra) in the matter."¹¹

﴿And guidance and mercy for a people who believe.﴾

﴿When the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent﴾. 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: We used to greet one another in prayer, saying "Peace be upon so-and-so, peace be upon so-and-so." Then this verse came: ﴿When the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent﴾, meaning during the prayer.

Abu Hurayra said: They used to speak during the prayer, and then this verse came and they were commanded to be silent.

al-Zuhri said: This verse was revealed concerning a young man from the Ansar. Whenever the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited something, he would recite it too. So this verse was revealed.

Dawud ibn Abi Hind narrated from Bashir ibn Jabir, who said: Ibn Mas'ud prayed and heard some people reciting along with the imam. When he finished he said: "Has it not yet come time for you to understand? Has it not yet come time for you to reflect? ﴿When the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent﴾, as Allah has commanded you."¹²

al-Hariri narrated from Talha ibn 'Ubayd Allah ibn Kuraiz, who said: I saw 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr and 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah talking while the reader was reciting. I said: "Will you not listen to the remembrance and attend to what is promised?" He said: They looked at me, then turned back to their conversation. I repeated it a second time, and they looked at me and said: "That is only during the prayer: ﴿When the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent.﴾"

Zayd ibn Aslam narrated from his father, from Abu Hurayra, who said: This verse was revealed concerning raising voices while they were behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the prayer.¹³

al-Kalbi said: They used to raise their voices in prayer until they heard mention of Paradise and Hell, so Allah the Exalted revealed this verse.

Qatada said: At the beginning when it was prescribed for them, they used to speak in the prayer about their needs. A man would come while they were praying and ask them: "How many have you prayed? How many remain?" So Allah the Mighty and Majestic revealed this verse.¹⁴

Ibn 'Abbas said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited in the silent prayer, and his companions recited behind him raising their voices, so they confused him, and this verse was revealed.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: The polytheists would come to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he prayed, and some of them would say to others in Mecca: ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it.⁠﴾ So Allah revealed a reply to them: ﴿When the Qur'an is recited...﴾

Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, 'Ata', 'Amr ibn Dinar, Zayd ibn Aslam, al-Qasim ibn Yasar and Shahr ibn Hawshab said: This is about the sermon: a command to be silent for the imam on Friday.

'Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak said: The evidence for the ruling of this verse concerning the Friday sermon is that you never see a preacher on the pulpit on Friday delivering a sermon who wants to recite a verse from the Qur'an without reciting this verse before the recitation of the Qur'an.

al-Hasan said: This is about the obligatory prayer and during remembrance (dhikr). Mujahid and 'Ata' said: Silence became obligatory in two situations: when a man recites the Qur'an while praying, and when the imam is delivering the sermon.

'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said: Silence is for every preacher's speech, and silence means attentive listening and observance.

The poet said:

"The imam said: 'Obey your leader's command,'
so we did not oppose, and we were silent as they said."¹⁵

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: This is about silence on the two festivals and on Friday, and in what the imam recites aloud.¹⁶

al-Zajjaj said: It is permissible that the meaning of His saying "listen" and "be silent" is: act by what it contains and do not transgress it, because the meaning of someone saying "Allah has heard" is: Allah has answered your supplication.

﴿And remember your Lord within yourself﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: By remembrance he means recitation during the prayer. ﴿Humbly (tadarru')﴾, aloud, ﴿and in fear (khifatan)﴾, ﴿and below the level of loudness﴾, below raising the voice, in a low tone and silence, so that those behind you may hear.

The people of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: ﴿And remember your Lord﴾: be admonished by the Qur'an and believe in its signs. ﴿And remember your Lord﴾ by obedience in what He commands you. ﴿(Tadarru')﴾: humility and submission. ﴿(Khifah)﴾: fear of His punishment. So when you recite, you supplicate to Allah, i.e., ﴿below the level of loudness﴾: a concealment, not a shout.¹⁷

Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj said: He was commanded to remember Him in the heart. And he is commanded to humble himself in supplication and submission.

Raising the voice in supplication is disliked [and the excessive shouting] in supplication.

As for His saying ﴿in the mornings and the evenings (al-ghuduwwi wa al-asal)⁠﴾, it means at dawn and in the evenings. The singular of "al-asal" is "asil," like "ayman" and "yamin." The people of language said: it is the period between the afternoon prayer and sunset.

﴿And do not be among the heedless.⁠﴾

﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord﴾ means the angels. The meaning is nearness through grace and mercy, not nearness in place or in reward.

al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: Allah may be worshipped by others than the angels in meaning. [Those from your Lord] received success and protection.

﴿They do not disdain﴾, meaning they do not act arrogantly or consider themselves great, ﴿from His worship﴾, ﴿and they glorify Him﴾, purify Him, remember Him and say "Glory be to Allah," ﴿and to Him they prostrate﴾, meaning they pray.

Mughira narrated from Ibrahim: If he wishes, he bows; if he wishes, he prostrates.¹⁸

When he finished he said: "Has it not yet come time for you to understand? Has it not yet come time for you to reflect? ﴿When the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent﴾, as Allah has commanded you."¹²

al-Hariri narrated from Talha ibn 'Ubayd Allah ibn Kuraiz, who said: I saw 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr and 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah talking while the reader was reciting. I said: "Will you not listen to the remembrance and attend to what is promised?" He said: They looked at me, then turned back to their conversation. I repeated it a second time, and they looked at me and said: "That is only during the prayer: ﴿When the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent.﴾"

Zayd ibn Aslam narrated from his father, from Abu Hurayra, who said: This verse was revealed concerning raising voices while they were behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the prayer.¹³

al-Kalbi said: They used to raise their voices in prayer until they heard mention of Paradise and Hell, so Allah the Exalted revealed this verse.

Qatada said: At the beginning when it was prescribed for them, they used to speak in the prayer about their needs. A man would come while they were praying and ask them: "How many have you prayed? How many remain?" So Allah the Mighty and Majestic revealed this verse.¹⁴

Ibn 'Abbas said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited in the silent prayer, and his companions recited behind him raising their voices, so they confused him, and this verse was revealed.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: The polytheists would come to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he prayed, and some of them would say to others in Mecca: ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it.⁠﴾ So Allah revealed a reply to them: ﴿When the Qur'an is recited...﴾

Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, 'Ata', 'Amr ibn Dinar, Zayd ibn Aslam, al-Qasim ibn Yasar and Shahr ibn Hawshab said: This is about the sermon: a command to be silent for the imam on Friday.

'Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak said: The evidence for the ruling of this verse concerning the Friday sermon is that you never see a preacher on the pulpit on Friday delivering a sermon who wants to recite a verse from the Qur'an without reciting this verse before the recitation of the Qur'an.

al-Hasan said: This is about the obligatory prayer and during remembrance (dhikr). Mujahid and 'Ata' said: Silence became obligatory in two situations: when a man recites the Qur'an while praying, and when the imam is delivering the sermon.

'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said: Silence is for every preacher's speech, and silence means attentive listening and observance.

The poet said:

"The imam said: 'Obey your leader's command,'
so we did not oppose, and we were silent as they said."¹⁵

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: This is about silence on the two festivals and on Friday, and in what the imam recites aloud.¹⁶

al-Zajjaj said: It is permissible that the meaning of His saying "listen" and "be silent" is: act by what it contains and do not transgress it, because the meaning of someone saying "Allah has heard" is: Allah has answered your supplication.

﴿And remember your Lord within yourself﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: By remembrance he means recitation during the prayer. ﴿Humbly (tadarru')﴾, aloud, ﴿and in fear (khifatan)﴾, ﴿and below the level of loudness﴾, below raising the voice, in a low tone and silence, so that those behind you may hear.

The people of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: ﴿And remember your Lord﴾: be admonished by the Qur'an and believe in its signs. ﴿And remember your Lord﴾ by obedience in what He commands you. ﴿(Tadarru')﴾: humility and submission. ﴿(Khifah)﴾: fear of His punishment. So when you recite, you supplicate to Allah, i.e., ﴿below the level of loudness﴾: a concealment, not a shout.¹⁷

Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj said: He was commanded to remember Him in the heart. And he is commanded to humble himself in supplication and submission.

Raising the voice in supplication is disliked [and the excessive shouting] in supplication.

As for His saying ﴿in the mornings and the evenings (al-ghuduwwi wa al-asal)⁠﴾, it means at dawn and in the evenings. The singular of "al-asal" is "asil," like "ayman" and "yamin." The people of language said: it is the period between the afternoon prayer and sunset.

﴿And do not be among the heedless.⁠﴾

﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord﴾ means the angels. The meaning is nearness through grace and mercy, not nearness in place or in reward.

al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: Allah may be worshipped by others than the angels in meaning. [Those from your Lord] received success and protection.

﴿They do not disdain﴾, meaning they do not act arrogantly or consider themselves great, ﴿from His worship﴾, ﴿and they glorify Him﴾, purify Him, remember Him and say "Glory be to Allah," ﴿and to Him they prostrate﴾, meaning they pray.

Mughira narrated from Ibrahim: If he wishes, he bows; if he wishes, he prostrates.¹⁸

﴿Indeed, my Guardian is Allah, who sent down the Book, and He takes charge of the righteous.﴾ "Alladhi" means: the One who will protect me and keep me from you.

﴿As for those you call upon besides Him, they cannot help you, nor can they help themselves.﴾ ﴿And if you call them to guidance, they do not hear. And you see them, O Muhammad, looking at you, but they do not see.﴾ "They" means the idols. This is like what the Arabs say: "My house looks at your house," meaning it faces it.

The Arabs also say: "If you come to such-and-such a place and the mountain looks at you, take right or left," meaning: it faces you.

Abu 'Ubayda narrated from al-Kisa'i, who said: "The wall looks at you when it is near you, where you can see it." From this is the poet's saying:

When the lands of Banu Tamim look,
with an eye or without the eye of Banu Sabah...¹

I heard Abu al-Qasim al-Habibi say: I heard Abu Zakariyya al-'Anbari say: The meaning is: "And you see them" as though they were looking at you, like His saying: ﴿And you see people drunken, though they are not drunken﴾² meaning: as though they were drunk. He reported about them using the masculine pronoun (hum), because they are shaped in the form of the sons of Adam, reporting about them by their actions.

﴿Take what is easy.﴾ Mujahid said: It means forgiveness of the people's characters and deeds, without searching them out.

Ibn al-Zubayr said: Allah did not reveal this verse except concerning the people's characters.

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi said: It means what is given to you freely from their wealth, the surplus of dependents and of everything. "So whatever they bring you freely, take it, and do not ask them about what is beyond that."

This was before the obligatory charity (zakat) was revealed. When the verse of charity was revealed, this verse was abrogated (naskh), and he was commanded to take it from them, willingly or by force.

﴿And enjoin what is good (al-'urf)﴾, meaning: what is known as good (al-ma'ruf). 'Isa ibn 'Umar recited "al-'urf" with two dammas, like "al-hilm," and both are dialectal variants. "Al-'urf" is what is known, and "al-'arifa" is every praiseworthy quality that the intellects approve and that souls find reassuring. The poet said:

Whoever does good will not lack one who repays him;
good deeds do not vanish between Allah and the people.³

'Ata' said: "Enjoin what is good" means: there is no god but Allah. ﴿And turn away from the ignorant﴾, meaning Abu Jahl and his companions. It was abrogated by the verse of the sword.

It is said that when this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Jibril: "What is this?" He said: "I do not know until I ask." Then he returned and said: "O Muhammad, your Lord commands you to join ties with the one who cuts you off, to give to the one who withholds from you, and to pardon the one who wronged you."⁴

The poet composed:

The noble qualities are in three;
whoever has them perfected is a man of virtue:
giving to the one who denies you, joining ties with
the one who cuts you off, and pardoning the one who transgresses against you.

Ja'far al-Sadiq said: "Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) with the noble qualities, and there is no verse in the Qur'an more comprehensive of the noble qualities than this verse."⁵

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: (May Allah have mercy on them both).⁶

'A'isha said: The noble qualities are ten: truthfulness of speech; truthfulness in courage in obedience to Allah; giving to the beggar; repaying a favor; joining ties of kinship; fulfilling trusts; honoring one's companion; honoring one's neighbor; hospitality to the guest; and at their head, modesty.⁷

Abu al-Qasim al-Hasan ibn Muhammad, mentioned above, recited to us: Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Saffar recited to us: Ibn Abi al-Dunya recited to us: Abu Ja'far al-Qurashi recited to me:

All matters will leave you and come to an end,
except praise, which remains for you.
If I were given the choice of every virtue,
I would choose nothing but the noble qualities.⁸

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: When this verse was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "How, O Lord, [with anger?]" Then it was revealed: ﴿And if an evil whisper from Satan should come to you, seek refuge in Allah.﴾ Meaning: it may afflict you, tempt you, deceive you, and present itself to you from Satan, a "nazgh" (an incitement).

Its root meaning is an eagerness toward corruption and evil. It is said: "His vein provoked (nazagha 'irquhu)" when it was agitated and stirred up. There are two forms: nazgh and nagh. It is said: "Beware of the nizaʼ and the nighaz," meaning those who incite discord.

Al-Zajjaj said: Nazgh is the least movement that comes from a human, and from Satan, the least whisper. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: I witnessed 'Uthman and 'Ali, and there was an incitement from Satan between them, so neither of them left anything for his companion. Then they did not part until each of them asked forgiveness for the other.⁹

﴿So seek refuge in Allah﴾, meaning: seek protection in Allah. ﴿Indeed He is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾

﴿Indeed, those who have feared Allah﴾, meaning the believers, ﴿when a touch from Satan afflicts them﴾, meaning: strikes them, ﴿a passing thought (ta'if) from Satan.﴾ Al-Nakha'i, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, al-A'mash, Ibn Yazid, al-Jahdari and Talha recited "tayf." The rest recited "ta'if." Both are dialectal variants, like "al-mayt" and "al-mayyit." Their meaning is the thing that comes around you. Some people distinguished between them. Abu 'Amr said: "Ta'if" is what circles around a thing, and "tayf" is the passing impulse, the whisper, the fleeting thought. Some Meccan scholars said: "Ta'if" is what the Satanic whisper circles around, and "tayf" is the flesh and the touch. It is permissible that "tayf" is a lightened form of "tayyif," like "hayyin" and "layyin." This is supported by the recitation of Sa'id ibn Jubayr with the doubled yā' ("tayyif").

Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿When a passing thought from Satan afflicts them﴾ means: an incitement from Satan.

al-Kalbi said: It means a sin. Mujahid said: It means anger.

﴿They remember﴾: they reflect, consider and recognize. Abu Rawq said: They supplicate humbly. In the recitation of 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr: "When a passing thought from Satan afflicts them, they [seek refuge]" (fa-amalu).

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: It is the man who becomes angry, then remembers Allah and restrains his rage. Layth reported from Mujahid: It is the man who intends a sin, then remembers Allah and leaves it. al-Suddi said: It means: if they slip, they repent. Muqatil said: If the God-fearing person is struck by an incitement from Satan, he remembers and recognizes that it is sinful, so he sees it clearly, and the incitement to disobey Allah is removed from him. ﴿Then they are seeing clearly﴾: they look at the places of their error through reflection and contemplation, [and turn away], so they refrain. The God-fearing person is one who desires [...] (an illegible word) and sees, so he refrains.

Then he mentioned the disbelievers, saying: ﴿But their brothers﴾ (i.e., the brothers of the devils, who are the disbelievers), ﴿the devils extend them in error, and then they do not cease.﴾ The devils extend them in error until they seek them out and increase them in misguidance.

The people of Medina recited "yumiddūnahum" with a damma on the yā' and a kasra on the mīm, and both are dialects with the same meaning. al-Jahdari recited "yumadiʼūnahum" in the form of "yufā'ilūnahum."

﴿Then they do not cease﴾, meaning: they do not doubt and do not incite. Ibn Zayd said: They do not grow weary and do not slacken.

Ibn 'Abbas said: Neither humans cease from the evil deeds they do, nor do the jinn refrain from them.

'Isa ibn 'Umar recited "yaqṣurūn" with a fatha on the yā' and a damma on the ṣād. "Qaṣara" and "aqṣara" are one (in meaning).

﴿And when you do not bring them a sign, O Muhammad,﴾ meaning the polytheists, ﴿they say: "Why do you not invent it?"⁠﴾ meaning: why did you not fabricate it and originate it from yourself and by your own choice? This was said by Qatada. Mujahid said: "Why did you not contrive it and bring it out from yourself?"

Ibn Zayd said: "Why do you not choose it and bring it from yourself?"

Ibn 'Abbas said: "Why did you not receive it from yourself, or why did you not narrate it and originate it?" Al-'Awfi reported from Ibn 'Abbas: "You forgot it and invented it from your Lord."

al-Dahhak said: "Why did you not take it yourself and bring it from heaven?" al-Farra' said: The Arabs say: "I fabricated the speech, composed it, improvised it, and adopted it" when a man makes it up from himself.

Ibn Zayd said: The Arabs say that speech only to pacify a man, and he had not prepared it for himself beforehand.

﴿Say, O Muhammad: "I only follow what is revealed to me from my Lord."⁠﴾ Then He said: ﴿This (the Qur'an) is insights (basa'ir), proofs, clarity and evidence from your Lord.﴾ Its singular is "basīra." Al-Zajjaj said: Paths from your Lord; and "al-basā'ir" are the paths of blood (i.e., veins).

al-Ju'fi said:

They went with their insights on their shoulders,
and my insight runs with it, a sturdy steed...¹⁰

They pass beyond my enmity. Its root meaning is the manifestation and establishment of a thing until a person sees it, is guided by it, and benefits from it. From this is said: "I have no insight (basīra) in the matter."¹¹

﴿And guidance and mercy for a people who believe.﴾

﴿When the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent﴾. 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: We used to greet one another in prayer, saying "Peace be upon so-and-so, peace be upon so-and-so." Then this verse came: ﴿When the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent﴾, meaning during the prayer.

Abu Hurayra said: They used to speak during the prayer, and then this verse came and they were commanded to be silent.

al-Zuhri said: This verse was revealed concerning a young man from the Ansar. Whenever the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited something, he would recite it too. So this verse was revealed.

Dawud ibn Abi Hind narrated from Bashir ibn Jabir, who said: Ibn Mas'ud prayed and heard some people reciting along with the imam. When he finished he said: "Has it not yet come time for you to understand? Has it not yet come time for you to reflect? ﴿When the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent﴾, as Allah has commanded you."¹²

al-Hariri narrated from Talha ibn 'Ubayd Allah ibn Kuraiz, who said: I saw 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr and 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah talking while the reader was reciting. I said: "Will you not listen to the remembrance and attend to what is promised?" He said: They looked at me, then turned back to their conversation. I repeated it a second time, and they looked at me and said: "That is only during the prayer: ﴿When the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent.﴾"

Zayd ibn Aslam narrated from his father, from Abu Hurayra, who said: This verse was revealed concerning raising voices while they were behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the prayer.¹³

al-Kalbi said: They used to raise their voices in prayer until they heard mention of Paradise and Hell, so Allah the Exalted revealed this verse.

Qatada said: At the beginning when it was prescribed for them, they used to speak in the prayer about their needs. A man would come while they were praying and ask them: "How many have you prayed? How many remain?" So Allah the Mighty and Majestic revealed this verse.¹⁴

Ibn 'Abbas said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited in the silent prayer, and his companions recited behind him raising their voices, so they confused him, and this verse was revealed.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: The polytheists would come to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he prayed, and some of them would say to others in Mecca: ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it.⁠﴾ So Allah revealed a reply to them: ﴿When the Qur'an is recited...﴾

Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, 'Ata', 'Amr ibn Dinar, Zayd ibn Aslam, al-Qasim ibn Yasar and Shahr ibn Hawshab said: This is about the sermon: a command to be silent for the imam on Friday.

'Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak said: The evidence for the ruling of this verse concerning the Friday sermon is that you never see a preacher on the pulpit on Friday delivering a sermon who wants to recite a verse from the Qur'an without reciting this verse before the recitation of the Qur'an.

al-Hasan said: This is about the obligatory prayer and during remembrance (dhikr). Mujahid and 'Ata' said: Silence became obligatory in two situations: when a man recites the Qur'an while praying, and when the imam is delivering the sermon.

'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said: Silence is for every preacher's speech, and silence means attentive listening and observance.

The poet said:

"The imam said: 'Obey your leader's command,'
so we did not oppose, and we were silent as they said."¹⁵

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: This is about silence on the two festivals and on Friday, and in what the imam recites aloud.¹⁶

al-Zajjaj said: It is permissible that the meaning of His saying "listen" and "be silent" is: act by what it contains and do not transgress it, because the meaning of someone saying "Allah has heard" is: Allah has answered your supplication.

﴿And remember your Lord within yourself﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: By remembrance he means recitation during the prayer. ﴿Humbly (tadarru')﴾, aloud, ﴿and in fear (khifatan)﴾, ﴿and below the level of loudness﴾, below raising the voice, in a low tone and silence, so that those behind you may hear.

The people of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: ﴿And remember your Lord﴾: be admonished by the Qur'an and believe in its signs. ﴿And remember your Lord﴾ by obedience in what He commands you. ﴿(Tadarru')﴾: humility and submission. ﴿(Khifah)﴾: fear of His punishment. So when you recite, you supplicate to Allah, i.e., ﴿below the level of loudness﴾: a concealment, not a shout.¹⁷

Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj said: He was commanded to remember Him in the heart. And he is commanded to humble himself in supplication and submission.

Raising the voice in supplication is disliked [and the excessive shouting] in supplication.

As for His saying ﴿in the mornings and the evenings (al-ghuduwwi wa al-asal)⁠﴾, it means at dawn and in the evenings. The singular of "al-asal" is "asil," like "ayman" and "yamin." The people of language said: it is the period between the afternoon prayer and sunset.

﴿And do not be among the heedless.⁠﴾

﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord﴾ means the angels. The meaning is nearness through grace and mercy, not nearness in place or in reward.

al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: Allah may be worshipped by others than the angels in meaning. [Those from your Lord] received success and protection.

﴿They do not disdain﴾, meaning they do not act arrogantly or consider themselves great, ﴿from His worship﴾, ﴿and they glorify Him﴾, purify Him, remember Him and say "Glory be to Allah," ﴿and to Him they prostrate﴾, meaning they pray.

Mughira narrated from Ibrahim: If he wishes, he bows; if he wishes, he prostrates.¹⁸

I would choose nothing but the noble qualities.⁸

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: When this verse was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "How, O Lord, [with anger?]" Then it was revealed: ﴿And if an evil whisper from Satan should come to you, seek refuge in Allah.﴾ Meaning: it may afflict you, tempt you, deceive you, and present itself to you from Satan, a "nazgh" (an incitement).

Its root meaning is an eagerness toward corruption and evil. It is said: "His vein provoked (nazagha 'irquhu)" when it was agitated and stirred up. There are two forms: nazgh and nagh. It is said: "Beware of the nizaʼ and the nighaz," meaning those who incite discord.

Al-Zajjaj said: Nazgh is the least movement that comes from a human, and from Satan, the least whisper. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: I witnessed 'Uthman and 'Ali, and there was an incitement from Satan between them, so neither of them left anything for his companion. Then they did not part until each of them asked forgiveness for the other.⁹

﴿So seek refuge in Allah﴾, meaning: seek protection in Allah. ﴿Indeed He is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾

﴿Indeed, those who have feared Allah﴾, meaning the believers, ﴿when a touch from Satan afflicts them﴾, meaning: strikes them, ﴿a passing thought (ta'if) from Satan.﴾ Al-Nakha'i, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, al-A'mash, Ibn Yazid, al-Jahdari and Talha recited "tayf." The rest recited "ta'if." Both are dialectal variants, like "al-mayt" and "al-mayyit." Their meaning is the thing that comes around you. Some people distinguished between them. Abu 'Amr said: "Ta'if" is what circles around a thing, and "tayf" is the passing impulse, the whisper, the fleeting thought. Some Meccan scholars said: "Ta'if" is what the Satanic whisper circles around, and "tayf" is the flesh and the touch. It is permissible that "tayf" is a lightened form of "tayyif," like "hayyin" and "layyin." This is supported by the recitation of Sa'id ibn Jubayr with the doubled yā' ("tayyif").

Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿When a passing thought from Satan afflicts them﴾ means: an incitement from Satan.

al-Kalbi said: It means a sin. Mujahid said: It means anger.

﴿They remember﴾: they reflect, consider and recognize. Abu Rawq said: They supplicate humbly. In the recitation of 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr: "When a passing thought from Satan afflicts them, they [seek refuge]" (fa-amalu).

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: It is the man who becomes angry, then remembers Allah and restrains his rage. Layth reported from Mujahid: It is the man who intends a sin, then remembers Allah and leaves it. al-Suddi said: It means: if they slip, they repent. Muqatil said: If the God-fearing person is struck by an incitement from Satan, he remembers and recognizes that it is sinful, so he sees it clearly, and the incitement to disobey Allah is removed from him. ﴿Then they are seeing clearly﴾: they look at the places of their error through reflection and contemplation, [and turn away], so they refrain. The God-fearing person is one who desires [...] (an illegible word) and sees, so he refrains.

Then he mentioned the disbelievers, saying: ﴿But their brothers﴾ (i.e., the brothers of the devils, who are the disbelievers), ﴿the devils extend them in error, and then they do not cease.﴾ The devils extend them in error until they seek them out and increase them in misguidance.

The people of Medina recited "yumiddūnahum" with a damma on the yā' and a kasra on the mīm, and both are dialects with the same meaning. al-Jahdari recited "yumadiʼūnahum" in the form of "yufā'ilūnahum."

﴿Then they do not cease﴾, meaning: they do not doubt and do not incite. Ibn Zayd said: They do not grow weary and do not slacken.

Ibn 'Abbas said: Neither humans cease from the evil deeds they do, nor do the jinn refrain from them.

'Isa ibn 'Umar recited "yaqṣurūn" with a fatha on the yā' and a damma on the ṣād. "Qaṣara" and "aqṣara" are one (in meaning).

﴿And when you do not bring them a sign, O Muhammad,﴾ meaning the polytheists, ﴿they say: "Why do you not invent it?"⁠﴾ meaning: why did you not fabricate it and originate it from yourself and by your own choice? This was said by Qatada. Mujahid said: "Why did you not contrive it and bring it out from yourself?"

Ibn Zayd said: "Why do you not choose it and bring it from yourself?"

Ibn 'Abbas said: "Why did you not receive it from yourself, or why did you not narrate it and originate it?" Al-'Awfi reported from Ibn 'Abbas: "You forgot it and invented it from your Lord."

al-Dahhak said: "Why did you not take it yourself and bring it from heaven?" al-Farra' said: The Arabs say: "I fabricated the speech, composed it, improvised it, and adopted it" when a man makes it up from himself.

Ibn Zayd said: The Arabs say that speech only to pacify a man, and he had not prepared it for himself beforehand.

﴿Say, O Muhammad: "I only follow what is revealed to me from my Lord."⁠﴾ Then He said: ﴿This (the Qur'an) is insights (basa'ir), proofs, clarity and evidence from your Lord.﴾ Its singular is "basīra." Al-Zajjaj said: Paths from your Lord; and "al-basā'ir" are the paths of blood (i.e., veins).

al-Ju'fi said:

They went with their insights on their shoulders,
and my insight runs with it, a sturdy steed...¹⁰

They pass beyond my enmity. Its root meaning is the manifestation and establishment of a thing until a person sees it, is guided by it, and benefits from it. From this is said: "I have no insight (basīra) in the matter."¹¹

﴿And guidance and mercy for a people who believe.﴾

﴿When the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent﴾. 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: We used to greet one another in prayer, saying "Peace be upon so-and-so, peace be upon so-and-so." Then this verse came: ﴿When the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent﴾, meaning during the prayer.

Abu Hurayra said: They used to speak during the prayer, and then this verse came and they were commanded to be silent.

al-Zuhri said: This verse was revealed concerning a young man from the Ansar. Whenever the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited something, he would recite it too. So this verse was revealed.

Dawud ibn Abi Hind narrated from Bashir ibn Jabir, who said: Ibn Mas'ud prayed and heard some people reciting along with the imam. When he finished he said: "Has it not yet come time for you to understand? Has it not yet come time for you to reflect? ﴿When the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent﴾, as Allah has commanded you."¹²

al-Hariri narrated from Talha ibn 'Ubayd Allah ibn Kuraiz, who said: I saw 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr and 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah talking while the reader was reciting. I said: "Will you not listen to the remembrance and attend to what is promised?" He said: They looked at me, then turned back to their conversation. I repeated it a second time, and they looked at me and said: "That is only during the prayer: ﴿When the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent.﴾"

Zayd ibn Aslam narrated from his father, from Abu Hurayra, who said: This verse was revealed concerning raising voices while they were behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the prayer.¹³

al-Kalbi said: They used to raise their voices in prayer until they heard mention of Paradise and Hell, so Allah the Exalted revealed this verse.

Qatada said: At the beginning when it was prescribed for them, they used to speak in the prayer about their needs. A man would come while they were praying and ask them: "How many have you prayed? How many remain?" So Allah the Mighty and Majestic revealed this verse.¹⁴

Ibn 'Abbas said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited in the silent prayer, and his companions recited behind him raising their voices, so they confused him, and this verse was revealed.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: The polytheists would come to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he prayed, and some of them would say to others in Mecca: ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it.⁠﴾ So Allah revealed a reply to them: ﴿When the Qur'an is recited...﴾

Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, 'Ata', 'Amr ibn Dinar, Zayd ibn Aslam, al-Qasim ibn Yasar and Shahr ibn Hawshab said: This is about the sermon: a command to be silent for the imam on Friday.

'Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak said: The evidence for the ruling of this verse concerning the Friday sermon is that you never see a preacher on the pulpit on Friday delivering a sermon who wants to recite a verse from the Qur'an without reciting this verse before the recitation of the Qur'an.

al-Hasan said: This is about the obligatory prayer and during remembrance (dhikr). Mujahid and 'Ata' said: Silence became obligatory in two situations: when a man recites the Qur'an while praying, and when the imam is delivering the sermon.

'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said: Silence is for every preacher's speech, and silence means attentive listening and observance.

The poet said:

"The imam said: 'Obey your leader's command,'
so we did not oppose, and we were silent as they said."¹⁵

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: This is about silence on the two festivals and on Friday, and in what the imam recites aloud.¹⁶

al-Zajjaj said: It is permissible that the meaning of His saying "listen" and "be silent" is: act by what it contains and do not transgress it, because the meaning of someone saying "Allah has heard" is: Allah has answered your supplication.

﴿And remember your Lord within yourself﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: By remembrance he means recitation during the prayer. ﴿Humbly (tadarru')﴾, aloud, ﴿and in fear (khifatan)﴾, ﴿and below the level of loudness﴾, below raising the voice, in a low tone and silence, so that those behind you may hear.

The people of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: ﴿And remember your Lord﴾: be admonished by the Qur'an and believe in its signs. ﴿And remember your Lord﴾ by obedience in what He commands you. ﴿(Tadarru')﴾: humility and submission. ﴿(Khifah)﴾: fear of His punishment. So when you recite, you supplicate to Allah, i.e., ﴿below the level of loudness﴾: a concealment, not a shout.¹⁷

Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj said: He was commanded to remember Him in the heart. And he is commanded to humble himself in supplication and submission.

Raising the voice in supplication is disliked [and the excessive shouting] in supplication.

As for His saying ﴿in the mornings and the evenings (al-ghuduwwi wa al-asal)⁠﴾, it means at dawn and in the evenings. The singular of "al-asal" is "asil," like "ayman" and "yamin." The people of language said: it is the period between the afternoon prayer and sunset.

﴿And do not be among the heedless.⁠﴾

﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord﴾ means the angels. The meaning is nearness through grace and mercy, not nearness in place or in reward.

al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: Allah may be worshipped by others than the angels in meaning. [Those from your Lord] received success and protection.

﴿They do not disdain﴾, meaning they do not act arrogantly or consider themselves great, ﴿from His worship﴾, ﴿and they glorify Him﴾, purify Him, remember Him and say "Glory be to Allah," ﴿and to Him they prostrate﴾, meaning they pray.

Mughira narrated from Ibrahim: If he wishes, he bows; if he wishes, he prostrates.¹⁸
